ii. The three basic substantial-insubstantial states (1) The substantial and insubstantial of the feet — the division of the feet's substantial and insubstantial is simply that one foot bears somewhat more and the other somewhat less. According to mechanical principles, if the centre of gravity of the body's weight is located in the middle third of the distance between the two legs, then both feet can have their footing, and this is called half-light half-heavy ① (as in Figure 9). If the centre of gravity goes beyond the range of the middle third, then the insubstantial foot, being too insubstantial, will produce the phenomenon of floating and swinging Figure 9 · Half-light half-heavy　　Figure 10 · Leaning-light leaning-heavy

  • ① "Half" means that the centre of gravity of the body's weight is within the middle third of the distance between the two legs; at this time both feet have their downward jin settled on the ground, only differing in lightness and heaviness, and so it is called half having footing, or half-light half-heavy; this is the correct posture.

· 30 · phenomena, becoming the morbid phenomenon of leaning-light leaning-heavy ① (as in Figure 10).

Moreover, in movement or in issuing jin, the movement must achieve curved storage with surplus. Even after issuing jin, the four limbs should still not be fully straightened. For once straightened, in exchanging substantial and insubstantial one must first change the straight into bent before one can reverse the extension and contraction. But if the hands and feet are in the posture of curved storage with surplus, then on contact they can rotate freely, and one need not divide one's attention amid the reversing, which is the foundation enabling the movement to become automatic.

In sum, in Taijiquan's requirement of substantial and insubstantial for the two feet, at whatever time and place there must be the exchange of this one insubstantial and one substantial, and one must especially gradually reduce the proportion so as to hasten the turning of substantial and insubstantial. If the two feet exchange substantial and insubstantial not quickly enough, they cannot adapt to the changes of the hands, and upper and lower cannot follow each other; they will then split into two branches, destroying the requirement that the movement be of the whole body as one family.

(2) The substantial and insubstantial of the hands — whenever the jin is carried to the hand and lifted in ward-off, that hand is insubstantial; when it is carried to the hand and sinks down, that hand is substantial. The movements of the two hands in Taijiquan, like the movements of the two legs, must also be divided into substantial and insubstantial; even when both hands press together doubly, as in the form Six Sealing and Four Closing, it is likewise divided by the four-six proportion. But the proportions of substantial and insubstantial for the hands differ somewhat from those for the legs: after one's skill has become refined, its proportions, apart from a few individual forms, all lie between three-seven and four-six, the proportions being large. This is laid down in order to achieve steadiness and relaxed quietness, with one side taking charge, so that one side is host and the other is guest. What is especially important is that not only must the limbs exchange nimbly, but intent and qi must exchange nimbly even more, so that intent and qi do not stagnate on one hand, especially the right hand.

(3) The substantial and insubstantial of hands and feet — the division of substantial and insubstantial that takes the most skill is that of the upper and lower of one hand and one foot. And what is most effective in health care and in combat is likewise this upper-lower division of substantial and insubstantial of one hand and one foot. This is the core of making the stepping achieve connecting and following.

  • ① "Leaning" means that the position of the centre of gravity has already gone beyond the range of the middle third, making one foot especially heavy while the other floats and swings on the ground, forming a leaning to one side; hence the other side is of course leaning-light. This is called leaning without footing, or leaning-light leaning-heavy, and is a kind of fault.

· 31 · Its requirement and method are: if the right hand sinks down and is substantial, then the right foot must be insubstantial; and when the right hand turns to the upper ward-off and is insubstantial, then the right foot follows the hand above and turns substantial. Doing this is called "dividing substantial and insubstantial with upper and lower following each other." Hence in the Taijiquan "Song of Hand-Pushing" it is said: "Ward-off, roll-back, press, and push must be done with care; when upper and lower follow each other, one is hard to invade" — one may well imagine its importance. Therefore, when practising the form, one must fully examine whether every movement has attained this requirement of upper and lower following each other. To take one round of practising the frame: the postures within are many and varied, and the changes of posture are so frequent that to achieve upper and lower following each other one must of course spend much effort before one can grasp it proficiently. In these changes, apart from changing substantial and insubstantial with the hand following the foot when stepping out, most are changes of substantial and insubstantial with the foot following the hand. In short, if one can achieve the upper-lower substantial and insubstantial of one hand and one foot, then the position of the centre of gravity will not go beyond the range of the middle third of the distance between the two legs, making both left and right legs have their footing; and thus the inner jin can attain central correctness. Once the inner jin is centrally correct, then one can support the eight directions. Reduced to the landing point of the foot on the ground, this kind of substantial and insubstantial is insubstantial-within-substantial and substantial-within-insubstantial. Only when one possesses this upper-and-lower-following substantial and insubstantial can the stepping be nimble and unclogged, advancing and retreating freely, and can one connect and follow the opponent without producing the morbid sign of losing and butting. At the same time, when pushing hands after proficiency, one need only pay attention to the one hand in contact with the opponent, while the other hand and both feet may thereby cultivate the habit of upper and lower following each other, without needing further divided attention; one can obtain the effect of automatic coordination, which is also the key to seeking stillness within movement and thereby attaining stillness.

Book page 32

III. The Grasping of Substantial and Insubstantial

III. The Grasping of Substantial and Insubstantial

As said above, Taijiquan takes the clear division of substantial and insubstantial and the eccentric moment produced by the shifting of the centre of gravity as its source of motive power; this is the most effort-saving mechanical action, and can make one tireless over long periods. In practising the form, one need only shift the centre of gravity once and one can set the movement going. The procedure of this training in substantial and insubstantial is: first the substantial and insubstantial of the two feet, next the substantial and insubstantial of the two hands, and finally, and most importantly, the upper-lower substantial and insubstantial of one hand and one foot.

· 32 · When Taijiquan practises one round of the frame, the two hands, in order to move in curved circles, must constantly change between sudden insubstantiality and sudden substantiality, thereby impelling the two feet to adjust their substantial and insubstantial in accordance with the substantial and insubstantial of the hands. Likewise, the two feet, in advancing and retreating, always step out insubstantially, and only on reaching their point do they settle and become substantial. This is the general stepping requirement of Taijiquan; hence the hands must change substantial and insubstantial following the substantial and insubstantial of the feet. All these belong to the requirement of upper following lower and lower following upper, of upper and lower following each other; in practising Taijiquan one must comply with this requirement and cultivate this habit. Through long and repeated practice, once it becomes a habit, then when a person comes one naturally produces the automatic "connecting", and when a person leaves one naturally produces the automatic "following", and one need no longer expend much intent in directing the movements.

Book page 33

IV. Light and Heavy, Floating and Sinking, and Substantial and Insubstantial

IV. Light and Heavy, Floating and Sinking, and Substantial and Insubstantial

The division of substantial and insubstantial, at first glance, is not a complicated matter, but in fact it is an extremely minute and multifarious learning process. Therefore, in order better to learn substantial and insubstantial, one must further understand the relation of the four — light, heavy, floating, sinking — to substantial and insubstantial. The boxing treatise says: "If one does not exhaustively study the hand of light, heavy, floating, and sinking, one will have the sigh of digging a well in vain without reaching the spring" — this shows its importance.

In order to grasp this substantial and insubstantial minutely, one should in each boxing form carefully feel it out, find out its defects, and correct them one by one. At this point there are six keys that must be grasped; having grasped these six keys, one can basically be a skilled hand rather than a faulty hand.

(1) One should be "half", not "leaning" — what is called "half" means that the eccentric distance of the body's centre of gravity has not gone beyond the range of the middle third of the distance between the two legs; this is a kind of eccentricity located within the square-and-circle, and is the standard for correctly dividing substantial and insubstantial. What is called "leaning" means that the eccentric distance of the body's centre of gravity has already gone beyond the above range, so that the eccentricity has gone out of the square-and-circle — this is because substantial and insubstantial have been divided too far. Therefore "half" is having footing and is not a fault, whereas "leaning" has no footing and is a fault. Hence in dividing substantial and insubstantial one should be "half", not "leaning". (As in Figure 11.)

· 33 · is having footing and is not a fault, whereas "leaning" has no footing and is a fault. Hence in dividing substantial and insubstantial one should be "half", not "leaning". (As in Figure 11.)

图 11
Diagram of Square and Circle (circle within square, square within circle; the diagram marks the circle-point, the square-point, the spiral line (circle), the opening line (square), the human body, and the region of movement)

(2) One should be "sinking", not "heavy" — what is called "heavy" means the phenomenon of sluggishness produced by over-filling. What is called "sinking" means that although it is a sinking down, one can still "of itself soar into emptiness"; that is to say, sinking is produced within upper and lower following each other: if the foot sinks down and is substantial, while the hand lifts up in ward-off and is insubstantial, then one can make substantial-within-insubstantial. Hence "sinking" is not a fault, whereas "heavy" is a fault (except for half-light half-heavy). Therefore in dividing substantial and insubstantial one should be "sinking", not "heavy".

(3) One should be "light", not "floating" — "light" is to make the movement manifest nimble lightness with footing within the square-and-circle; whereas "floating" is going out of the square-and-circle, making the heel float up and drift without footing — that is, being insubstantial to excess. Hence floating is a morbid sign. Therefore in dividing substantial and insubstantial one should be "light", not "floating".

(4) The three faultless substantial-and-insubstantial — in practising the form one should learn and achieve the three faultless substantial-and-insubstantial: "double light①", "double sinking", and "half-light half-heavy". Among these three

  • ① Under the movement of qi in which the intent is empty-and-nimble without delusion and clear brightness resides in the person, one drums and surges the top jin; above, the two arms are linked, and below, the two legs follow; substantial and insubstantial differ only by a minute amount, yet they can naturally and nimbly convert — this is double light, and therefore it is not a fault.

· 34 · faultless substantial-and-insubstantial, the skills of "double light" and "double sinking" are comparatively fine and hard to do; if not done well, there is the possibility of drifting into "double floating①" (hands insubstantial and feet also insubstantial) and "double heavy" (hands substantial and feet also substantial), and to this one must give full attention. In particular, the skilled hand of "double light" and "double sinking" and the faulty hand of "double floating" and "double heavy" differ by only a hair's breadth in the shifting of hands and feet; hence one should all the more guard against the possibility that this hair's-breadth difference becomes a thousand-li error.

(5) The separating hand is an important measure for remedying leaning-heavy and leaning-floating② — in practising alone

  • ① Double floating is when the two hands are insubstantial, and the two feet, because of excessive great insubstantiality and great substantiality, are such that in the process of movement not only does that insubstantial foot float up, but even that over-substantial foot, when changing, is dragged so that one stands unsteadily and floats up, so that the whole body drifts without footing — this becomes double floating, and is therefore a fault.
  • ② What is called leaning-heavy leaning-floating arises from the hand and foot on the same side being both insubstantial above and below, or both substantial above and below, so that the jin is biased to one side. Therefore the dividing of substantial and insubstantial with upper and lower following each other is precisely proposed in order that leaning-heavy and leaning-floating may not occur.

· 35 · practice one can achieve the requirement of changing substantial and insubstantial without going out of the corner — that is, one will not go out of the square-circle and produce leaning-heavy and leaning-floating substantial-and-insubstantial. But when pushing hands with a person, two sides are already involved, and one absolutely cannot, by subjective wish, one-sidedly think that one can refrain from going out of the corner and thereby refrain from going out of the corner. If the opponent uses the separating hand of pluck and rend to seize hard and strike hard, then one will sometimes unavoidably go out of the corner. Therefore one cannot but use the separating hand to remedy this out-of-the-corner substantial-and-insubstantial, so as to make it return again within the square-circle and attain the substantial-and-insubstantial of half-light half-heavy. For example: the right hand goes out of the corner and the left hand strikes out; if the person meets the left hand, then the right hand can again return within the four cardinal directions of the square-circle. This is the technique of remedying one's own substantial-and-insubstantial going out of the corner. (As in Figure 12.)

(6) To do substantial and insubstantial well, do not forget the separating hand — for example, when pushing hands, if the opponent is one who greatly opens and greatly spreads and leans and tilts, and often thinks to use the out-of-corner technique to control others, then at this time, if one does not dare or is not accustomed to use the separating hand to deal with his separating hand, but still thinks to use the four cardinal directions to deal with his four corners, and with him to stick, adhere, and draw circles, · 36 · pushing ceaselessly, then such a movement goes against the rule of corner hand dealing with corner hand, and will make one unconsciously produce the substantial-and-insubstantial of leaning-heavy and leaning-floating; one may say this is a defect produced by being habituated to using the four cardinal directions. Therefore the boxing treatise says: "Pluck, rend, elbow, shoulder are all the more marvellous; in doing them one need not spend mental effort" — this precisely explains the importance of the corner hand. If one forgets the grasp of the corner hand, then the leaning-heavy and leaning-floating of substantial and insubstantial cannot be corrected, and moreover one will be impelled further to go out of the corner. This is the defect produced by being habituated to the four cardinal directions and forgetting the four corners, becoming a "one-legged" person.

In order conveniently to grasp the fourth characteristic, its main points are summarized as follows.

(1) Clearly distinguish the three main substantial-and-insubstantial: namely the substantial-and-insubstantial of the feet, the substantial-and-insubstantial of the hands, and the substantial-and-insubstantial of one hand and one foot.

(2) Pay attention to adjusting the substantial-and-insubstantial of hand and foot in the left hand and left foot, and the right hand and right foot — this is the main key to "when upper and lower follow each other, one is hard to invade".

(3) According to the principles of light, heavy, floating, and sinking, constantly examine the defects in one's own division of substantial and insubstantial.

(4) One must achieve the three faultless substantial-and-insubstantial of double light, double sinking, and half-light half-heavy; this requires constant attention and long training before it can be formed.

(5) When pushing hands, do not forget the principle of "corner hand dealing with corner hand". The four-cardinal hand and the four-corner hand must convert into each other, and both must be practised.

Fifth Characteristic: The Joined-Segment Continuous Movement of Waist and Spine Leading, with Inner and Outer Mutually Fitting

Fifth Characteristic: The Joined-Segment Continuous Movement of Waist and Spine Leading, with Inner and Outer Mutually Fitting

The boxing manual lays down:

(1) "The waist and spine are the first rulers; when one moves, nothing does not move";

(2) "The whole body, segment by segment, is strung together, not allowing the slightest interruption";

· 37 · (3) "If one wishes the whole body to be one family, one must first have the whole body free of defects";

(4) "Move the qi like a nine-bend pearl, so that there is no subtle place it does not reach".

From the above four provisions one can see that, in order to attain "when one moves, all move", one must take the waist and spine as the centre, because the waist is the central axis of the left-right parallel turning, and the spine is the foundation of the up-down bending. Since the movements of Taijiquan require that when one moves all move, then on the movement path one cannot merely turn horizontally left and right, nor can one exclusively do bending movements up and down, forward and back; rather one must unite waist and spine so that the path of movement forms a spatial curve that is at once left-right and also up-down, forward-back, thereby establishing the foundation of "when one moves, all move". That is to say, only through taking waist and spine as the centre can one cause the nine main movement joints of the whole body② to be strung together in sequence. Moreover, one must achieve whole-body freedom from defects, strung together like a nine-bend round pearl; only thus can one's skill advance to the stage of the whole body as one family. Therefore the joined-segment continuous movement with waist and spine leading and inner and outer mutually fitting becomes the fifth characteristic of Taijiquan.

Book page 38

I. The Essence of Joined-Segment Continuity

I. The Essence of Joined-Segment Continuity

In order to make clear the essence of joined-segment continuity, let us take the lower half of the body as an example for explanation. When the jin starts from the heel, passes through the ankle joint, circles around the calf and rises to the knee joint, then from the knee joint rotates and rises, circling the thigh to the hip joint, and one can do this without the slightest interruption — this is called the joined-segment continuity of the lower half of the body. This shows that the so-called continuity is not only moving at the joints, but should make the whole leg circle and rise in motion. If one does not pass through the large and small legs, but moves only through the joints of ankle, knee, hip, and so on, then that belongs to a movement leaping from one segment to another, and this is a kind of "zero-break jin". Therefore only the jin that rises through the large and small legs is the true "continuous jin"③.

  • ① The nine main joints refer to: neck, spine, waist, hip, knee, ankle, shoulder, elbow, and wrist.
  • ② "Zero-break jin" is only joint movement, whereas "continuous jin" is muscle and joint moving together.

· 38 · Once the continuous jin is made clear, one can find the point of application of force. If the leg is front-bowed and back-collapsed without left-right rotation, then no matter how one tries it is impossible to string joints and muscles together; at this time one can only manifest the joint's contraction and release, which has no direct relation to the lengthening of the muscle. If the arm straightens and retracts directly, the situation is likewise. Therefore this requirement of continuity cannot be attained except by using the reeling-silk spiral-style rising.

Book page 39

II. The Relation of "When One Moves, All Move" to Waist and Spine

II. The Relation of "When One Moves, All Move" to Waist and Spine

The movements of Taijiquan first require that the nine main external joints can move in sequence and in continuity, for only thus can the internal organs be caused to produce a "massaging" action. When practising the form one must absolutely not have a few joints moving while other joints do not move. In order to make all the body's joints move in sequence and in full, one must find on the human body its central link and use it to lead the various joints to move in sequence; only thus will the movement become comparatively simple. Otherwise, one would have to use mental effort to attend to nine joints moving segment by segment together, which would cause one to attend to this and lose that, bustling without rest, and not only would one fail to attain the goal of continuous all-movement, but one would also lose the requirement of seeking stillness within movement.

We know that the two organs, waist and spine, occupy the middle of the human body; they naturally · 39 · possess the function of a central axis. Therefore, if one can make waist and spine cooperate with the spiral movement of the third characteristic, one can attain the requirement of joined-segment continuity; hence in Taijiquan the waist and spine are called the first rulers. Because of this central axis, the two hands can use the unity of centrifugal and centripetal force to achieve "when moving then separating, when still then joining" (as in Figure 13).

Book page 40

III. Joined-Segment Continuity and Strengthening the Joints

III. Joined-Segment Continuity and Strengthening the Joints

When Taijiquan has been practised to the point of joined-segment continuity, one can then attain the skill of the whole body as one family. Having formed this skill, one need only simply move very slightly, and one can make all parts of the body, inner and outer, move in coordination. This movement of continuity through the various joints can strengthen the joints and prevent them from degenerating. According to the laws of human physiology, regular joint activity helps preserve the normal structure of the cartilage tissue on the joint surfaces; if one does not often move, the cartilage tissue will undergo the degenerative action of fibrous change. If one does not move for a long time, its accessory organs will further harden, and thus a stiff state of immobile joints is formed. The cause of these pathological changes lies in the decline of the secretion of the synovial fluid that lubricates the joint surfaces.

From this one can see that the requirement of joined-segment continuity in Taijiquan plays an important role in strengthening joint function. In general, in practising Taijiquan one first seeks extension, and extended movement also enlarges the range of the human skeleton's activity. Therefore, when practising Taijiquan, a series of sounds often comes from the joints, making one feel relaxed; this shows that the joints have been exercised. Not only can this preserve the normal function of the joints, but it can also make the function of the bones steadily increase and accelerate the blood supply to the joints and their surroundings; hence even in old age one may step as briskly as a youth.

IV. The Adjustment of Joint Mobility

Although Taijiquan requires joined-segment continuity, with one movement moving all, nevertheless the mobility of its movements · 40 · is of varying size. The influence of a person's daily movements on the joints is uneven: among the nine joints, the one that turns most easily and most often is the wrist joint, and the one that turns least and least often is the spine. Yet the requirement of joined-segment continuity in Taijiquan is exactly contrary to this: it requires that the wrist joint move as little as possible, while the spine is required to lengthen and to move rather more — that is, the mobility of straightening and bending must be made greater. When the mobility of the wrist joint is reduced, one is forced to enlarge the body method to help attain the requirement of joined-segment continuity, and is forced to take waist and spine as ruler; otherwise one cannot turn smoothly and freely. If the mobility of the wrist joint is not reduced, then at one turn of the wrist a movement can easily turn and slip past without relation to the spine, and of course the waist moves little. Therefore the famous masters of Taijiquan often say: "In practising Taijiquan one should practise on the body, not on the hands." As for the wrist joint, one must reduce its mobility, forcing every movement to use the body method and to come out from the waist and spine.

The author had a friend who had practised Taijiquan for years, but paid attention only to hand technique, and his movement did not reach the body; in movement one saw only the arms moving, while the body was like a wooden stick, advancing and retreating with the stepping. Later, on another's advice, he used two pairs of thin boards to clamp his two wrists (four pieces in all), bored two holes in each end of the boards, and tied the boards with rubber bands, allowing the wrist only a small degree of bending. After practising thus for no long time, he transferred the former movement of the hands onto the body; once it reached the body, then when one moved all moved, and the requirement of joined-segment continuity also made comparatively good progress, the temper also gradually surged, and the body and limbs produced the flavour of round livingness like a pearl. This is the result of reducing the mobility of the wrist joint in order to raise the body method.

V. The Grasping of Joined-Segment Continuity

V. The Grasping of Joined-Segment Continuity
图 15
Diagram of the inclination of the curved surface of Taijiquan movement (the diagram marks the horizontal plane of movement, the vertical plane of movement, the planar movement path, and the oblique angle 0° < α < 90°)

In movement one must use the waist and spine as the motor, with the waist and spine as the centre; only thus can one practise well the skill of joined-segment continuity. And in order to make waist and spine the ruler, not attending to this and losing that and not dispersing one's thought, one can only use the centrifugal force possessing an angle of inclination to initiate the movement (Figure 15); only then can one naturally carry the jin onto the waist and spine. Therefore when practising the frame one must certainly cultivate this habit of movement, so that in movement one does not disperse one's mental attention; not only can one achieve the movement of waist-and-spine leading, but one can also achieve stillness within movement. "When moving then separating, when still then joining" describes the action of centrifugal force's "moving-separating" and "still-joining". Although the centrifugal force makes the two arms spiral apart simultaneously, yet because the two arms are linked, within the opening there is still concealed the inner jin of closing. This belongs to the opening-within-concealed-closing of the whole body. Secondly, because it is not direct opening and direct closing, the arms also possess spiral-style opening; this is elbow-closing-wrist-opening and wrist-closing-elbow-opening, the opening-within-concealed-closing and closing-within-concealed-opening. The former is the mutual concealment of the whole body's opening and closing, the latter the mutual concealment of the arms' opening and closing. This opening-within-concealed-closing and closing-within-concealed-opening of the whole body and the arms is the concrete manifestation of the "Taiji" diagram (yin and yang). Only when one has formed this skill can one be free in length and breadth, front and back, finding the source on left and right, rotating freely on contact, changing in ten thousand ways, providing favourable conditions for training both inner and outer, and it is also the foundation for removing the four faults in combat of "butting, collapsing, losing, resisting" (as in Figure 13).

The first route of Chen-style Taijiquan is mainly movement jin. In the process of moving jin, transforming jin is simultaneously produced, and after transforming one must issue jin; this is the law of movement development. Modern Taijiquan, revised for health purposes, is almost entirely moving jin, with the issuing of jin largely deleted.

· 42 · But Taijiquan was originally a boxing that used moving and issuing together, and hence the eight gates and five steps① were constituted. Therefore some people change the bright jin of issuing jin into hidden jin, so as to attain the intent of issuing jin without the form of issuing jin — that is, changing issuing jin into releasing jin, in order to lower the rigidity of the issuing jin and suit the requirements of physical training. What is called issuing jin means: beneath sinking the shoulders and dropping the elbows, guiding the various inner jins of curved storage with surplus to be transmitted from the spine and back to the arms and then sent out. Therefore the boxing manual lays down: "The jin is issued from the spine" — that is, it is issued by the spine's undoing its buckle. Only this kind of issuing jin is centrally correct jin; it is issued by the whole body converging all the various joints. Therefore the principle of joined-segment continuity must run through moving jin, issuing jin, and releasing jin alike, because the moving jin of joined-segment continuity is precisely the foundation of the issuing jin of joined-segment continuity. Apart from the fact that issuing jin is somewhat unsuitable for the aged and the weak, if young and strong people can practise to the point of being capable in both moving and issuing, not only can they form the eight-gate functions of the four cardinal and four corner directions, but it is also greatly beneficial for strengthening physical strength.

From this one can see that the moving jin of joined-segment continuity not only can lay the foundation for the skill of the whole body as one family, but can also provide the conditions for the issuing jin of joined-segment continuity. Issuing jin must be joined-segment continuous in order to strengthen its jin, concentrating the jin in the spine and back and then issuing it. At the same time, this in turn promotes the movement; hence the two interact and mutually increase each other, and therefore they have an extremely good effect on both health and combat.

In order conveniently to grasp the fifth characteristic, its essentials are now summarized as follows.

(1) Waist and spine united as the central axis, and the arm movements must have an angle of inclination (about 45 degrees);

(2) The "moving separation" and "still joining" produced by the central axis are the central key to using centrifugal force to attain continuity;

(3) Opening-within-concealed-closing and closing-within-concealed-opening are the concrete

· 43 · manifestation;

(4) The joined-segment continuity of issuing jin is the means of strengthening the continuity of moving jin;

(5) Reducing the mobility of the wrist joint is a necessary means of raising the effect of the body method.

Sixth Characteristic: The "One Breath Accomplished" Movement of Unbroken Connection and Endless Surging

Sixth Characteristic: The "One Breath Accomplished" Movement of Unbroken Connection and Endless Surging

The boxing manual lays down:

(1) "Going and returning must have folding and piling, advancing and retreating must have conversion";

(2) "Gathering is precisely releasing, releasing is precisely gathering";

(3) "When jin breaks the intent does not break, when intent breaks the spirit can connect";

(4) "Like the great Long River, surging endlessly, accomplished in one breath".

From the above four provisions one can see that Taijiquan is not satisfied with "when one moves, all move", but further requires that in practising the whole round of the frame one can further achieve accomplishment in one breath, with the inner jin unbroken. This is yet another method of increasing the amount of movement. Its concrete method is: in the hand technique, when going and returning are met, folding and piling must be fitted in; in the stepping, when advance and retreat are met, conversion must be fitted in; in opening and closing, gathering and releasing, there must be the intent and jin of "gathering is precisely releasing and releasing is precisely gathering". Of course, this characteristic, like the fifth, is realized with the aid of the spiral reeling-silk movement. If after issuing jin a phenomenon of broken jin appears, one must continue the remaining intent of this issuing jin. If by chance the intent also breaks①, then one must use the remaining spirit of intent and jin to continue it. In order to do this, the jin must have folding, piling, and conversion, and the movement must use intent and not force, so that the body method of unified gathering and releasing is like the endless surging of the waters of the Long River,

  • ① What is called breaking of intent means that intent and movement are disjointed, inner and outer not one, the intent galloping outward and the movement without a master.

· 44 · with no room in between for unloading the jin, nor any time of intent-galloping, and thus one can naturally attain the requirement of accomplishment in one breath. Therefore the "one breath accomplished" movement of unbroken connection and endless surging can serve as the sixth characteristic of Taijiquan.

Book page 45

I. The Realization of "Accomplishment in One Breath"

I. The Realization of "Accomplishment in One Breath"

This characteristic is, following the fifth characteristic, a concrete measure for further increasing the amount of movement on the basis of "when one moves, nothing does not move". The fifth characteristic emphasizes the requirement that the nine main joints must move all when one moves, thereby making the movement organs and the internal organs unite inner and outer, in order to raise the amount of movement of each boxing form. The sixth characteristic mainly requires, on the basis of "when one moves, all move", that from the first movement of a round of the frame right up to the end of practising the round of the frame, there be no place in between for unloading jin and no time of broken jin, nor any occurrence of dull spirit or thinking of other things, and still less any manifestation of taking a breather or departing from intent; rather one must achieve unbroken connection from beginning to end, wave-like surging and rising without cease — that is to say, one must accomplish a whole round of the frame in one breath. After this increase in the amount of movement, the calculation of the mobility of a whole round of the frame after practice should be the movement of the nine joints multiplied by the movements of one frame; supposing the frame's boxing forms to be seventy-two, then after practising a whole round of the frame one will have accomplished six hundred and forty-eight units of momentum in one breath. This is an outstanding and special creation of our ancestors in the field of physical culture. But in order to do this complex and ever-changing movement with unbroken connection from beginning to end, in broad terms one must accomplish the following two aspects.

(1) In hand technique — in movement, whenever a movement of one going and one returning is met, between the going and returning one must use folding and piling to fill the interval, so that the two movements, front and back, can be joined in a curved and gentle way. The method of this folding and piling is: when the movement has reached its end and one is about to do the next movement, if the next movement is to go downward and forward, then one must first fold once upward, then pile once backward, and then continue to do the next boxing form; thus one joins · 45 · naturally and in a curved and gentle way with the jin of the next movement. This is the statement laid down in the boxing treatise: "When the intent wishes to go up it must first lodge below, when the intent wishes to go forward it must first lodge behind." Doing this not only joins the jin of the former boxing form with the latter, but also makes the next boxing form, owing to the acceleration of the former boxing form, more steady and strengthened — exactly like the returning-tip brush technique in writing large characters with a brush. Therefore in Taijiquan movement, apart from a movement that can be completed within one circle, if in the movement there is a going and a returning (as at the junction of two boxing forms), then folding and piling must be added before the jin of the previous movement can be threaded without the slightest interruption into the next movement. This is the method of attaining unbroken connection in hand technique through folding and piling.

(2) In stepping — whenever moving the step to advance or retreat, between them one uses a "conversion" to fill the interval, so that the stepping before and after can likewise be joined in a curved and gentle way. The method of this conversion is: in stepping forward or retreating backward, one must not advance and retreat directly in a straight line; rather one must fit a conversion into the passage from the previous step to the next step. This conversion is the two steps of gaze and glance among the five steps of Taijiquan①. With the converting step of gaze and glance, not only can the jin of the legs be joined powerfully, but also the legs can be kept from leaving the reeling silk, and can be united in consistency above and below with the reeling silk of the two arms, performing the continuous function of movement arising from the heel and taking form at the fingers.

Within the entire routine of Taijiquan there are unceasing goings and returnings, and hence also unceasing foldings and pilings. With folding and piling fitted into the movement, practising the form shows a feeling of lingering attachment, producing an attitude of seeming-relaxed-yet-not-relaxed, about-to-extend-yet-not-extended, and manifesting the wave-like surging and rising appearance, as if one wave has passed and another wave surges without cease.

Within one round of the Taijiquan frame there are unceasing advances and retreats, and also unceasing conversions. With conversions fitted in between advance and retreat, advance and retreat are no longer direct advance and direct retreat,

  • ① The gaze-and-glance stepping is so described by the two words "gaze and glance" of the eyes because Taijiquan moves on the principle that the step follows the body's turn and the body follows the eye's movement; hence the name. Left is gaze, right is glance.

· 46 · but can manifest a meandering whirl and endless generation. When we practise the form on muddy ground, after finishing one round of the frame many circles of the heel may be left on the mud; these are the correct traces left by the gaze-and-glance two steps of this conversion.

In short, when between going and returning the arms have folding and piling, and between advancing and retreating the legs have conversion, then not only can the inner jin before and after be joined, but also the jin used in the processes of going-and-returning and advancing-and-retreating can all be round jin, so that the faults of butting-and-resisting and losing-and-collapsing do not occur, and the two opposites of going-and-returning and advancing-and-retreating can also be unified.

II. Examples of Famous Masters Performing the Form

II. Examples of Famous Masters Performing the Form

Around 1914, at the close of the annual meeting of the former Beijing Physical Education Research Society, martial artists of every style in the whole city — such as Ji Zixiu, Zhang Ce, Shang Yunxiang, Wang Maozhai, Xu Yusheng, and others — took part in an entertainment performance. In the Taijiquan field at that time, Yang Chengfu and Wu Jianquan performed Taijiquan together. Both used the large frame; in performing, the two made the audience feel only that they advanced and retreated amid finding the source on left and right, surging ceaselessly without cease, as if standing on a small rowboat crossing the Long River; their movements were on the surface extremely soft and pliant, yet within showed contained firmness and hardness; slow when just at the square, fast when reaching the circle, coordinating opening and closing with the utmost evenness and clarity, like a jade ring without end, so that one could not see clearly where the junction lay. In their advancing and retreating they did not appear to be advancing and retreating, and one felt only that they were step by step changing posture; the time to finish the performance was about eight minutes and more, and all present sighed in admiration, deeming it the utmost to behold.

That the famous masters could attain this profound and correct requirement in walking the frame was of course mainly the result of their diligent study and hard practice, with skill brought home. But if within it the folding and piling of going and returning and the conversion of advancing and retreating were lacking, it would be difficult to attain such ceaseless surging and accomplishment in one breath.

III. Spirit-and-Qi Surging and Accomplishment in One Breath①

III. Spirit-and-Qi Surging and Accomplishment in One Breath①

How, from the aspect of posture, to achieve unbroken connection has been stated above. This section focuses on describing how, from the aspect of spirit and qi, to attain unbroken connection, thereby making inner and outer one and truly attaining unbroken connection.

To examine whether the spirit and qi have broken, one need only look at whether the practitioner's spirit and qi are dull or surging; in other words, if the practitioner's spirit and qi, following the movement, manifest a surging bearing, that proves that at this moment this person has already poured his intent into the movement, proving that he is practising the form with intent; even if on the surface it looks as if the jin has broken, if consciousness still exists within the movement, one can only say that his inner jin has weakened in the movement, and cannot say the jin has broken. Therefore when practising walking the frame, one should pay attention to grasping the surging characteristic of spirit and qi, because this is the sole sign indicating that the inner jin is unbroken. Therefore from the very beginning of practising Taijiquan one should pay attention to lodging the inner intent and the outer spirit within the movement, without the slightest interruption; over time this can become a habit, so that if one does not walk the frame then nothing, but once one walks the frame, the spirit and qi must surge without cease, and the thought has no leisure to wander. In this way, even if by chance the thought wanders, one can still preserve the existence of the spirit as much as possible, and can quickly eliminate the phenomenon of broken jin and galloping intent.

IV. The Categories of Jin and Accomplishment in One Breath

The Taijiquan "Explanation of Correct Practice" says: "Taiji is the circle: no matter up, down, left, or right, one does not leave this circle. Taiji is the square: no matter up, down, left, or right, one does not leave this square. The circle's

  • ① What is here called "spirit-and-qi surging" differs somewhat from the "spirit-and-qi drumming-and-surging" of the first characteristic. "Spirit-and-qi drumming-and-surging" states that in movement one must drum and surge one's spirit and qi within the application of the eight gate categories of jin, which in turn strengthens the inner movement of intent and qi. "Spirit-and-qi surging" means cultivating, in ordinary movement, the habit of spirit-and-qi surging: if one does not move, then nothing; but when one moves, the spirit and qi surge following the movement, showing that the inner intent has not left the movement and has not galloped outward.

· 48 · going out and coming in, the square's advancing and retreating, follow the round's gathering and the square's going and coming. The square is extension, the round is compactness①; the ultimate of the square-and-round rule — who can go beyond this?" This is the origin of Taijiquan's requirement that square and round generate each other. In the beginning of learning Taijiquan, all movements are required to be round; even the very smallest turning is required to move in a round path drawing a circle. Concerning the round, much has been said above, but one point should still be pointed out: after one's skill has been practised to a fairly proficient degree, when the movement reaches its end point, one should manifest the category of jin prescribed for this boxing form; and to manifest the category of jin, one must show squareness within the round movement — in other words, if one wishes to manifest the category of jin in the course of movement, one must have the square. Therefore the boxing treatise says: "Only round without square is slippery boxing; only square without round is hard boxing."

The boxing treatise also says: "Folding and releasing attained in timely centrality is the root of civil arts; storing and issuing properly suited to what is fitting is the foundation of martial affairs"; it also says: "Exhalation is opening, is issuing; inhalation is closing, is storing. For with inhalation one naturally can lift up, and can also lift a person up; with exhalation one naturally can sink down, and can also send a person out. This is to move the qi by intent, not to make the qi by force." This says that when skill reaches a profound height one need no longer use the posture of great opening and great closing to store and issue, but can store and release merely by using the expansion and contraction of muscle and skin. In Taijiquan terminology this is the function of "inch jin", and it is also the foundation of qigong. Having reached this skill, one need no longer worry about the occurrence of interruption and continuation, because at this time one has already reached the lofty realm where square and round generate each other.

In order conveniently to grasp this characteristic, its essentials are specially summarized as follows.

(1) When a movement has going and returning, folding and piling must be fitted in — this is a necessary measure for attaining unbroken connection in hand technique.

(2) When the body has advance and retreat, conversion must be fitted in — this is in stepping

The latter refers to the practice of Taijiquan beginning by enlarging one's circle and then, as one's skill becomes profound, compacting the circle. What the former refers to is: "On exhalation, the body and limbs expand, forming extension and attaining the releasing jin of the square"; "on inhalation, the body and limbs contract, forming compactness and attaining the ward-off jin of the round".

· 49 · a necessary measure for attaining unbroken connection.

(3) When the jin breaks, the intent must be present; when the intent does not arrive, the spirit must be present — this is the method of remedying a broken jin.

(4) If one can walk the frame with spirit-and-qi surging, that proves one has already poured intent into the movement. Intent being present is the sign of unbroken inner jin.

(5) The mutual generation of square and round in Taiji jin is produced from "exhalation is extension, is the square" and "inhalation is compactness, is the round".

Seventh Characteristic: The Firmness-and-Softness-Mutually-Aiding Movement from Softness to Firmness and from Firmness to Softness

Seventh Characteristic: The Firmness-and-Softness-Mutually-Aiding Movement from Softness to Firmness and from Firmness to Softness

The boxing manual lays down:

(1) "Move the jin like steel tempered a hundred times; what hardness can it not break?" — "Extremely soft, and then extremely firm and hard".

(2) "Outwardly cultivate softness, inwardly contain firmness and hardness; constantly seek softness on the outside, and over time one can naturally obtain firmness and hardness within; it is not intentional firmness and hardness, but truly intentional softness."

(3) "Taijiquan must absolutely not lose its pliancy. In the going and returning of the whole body, take spirit, essence, intent, and qi as the foundation; with long use it will naturally run through."

(4) "The work of moving jin: first transform hardness into softness, then practise softness into firmness. When it reaches its utmost, it is both soft and firm. When firm and soft attain the mean, then yin and yang are seen. Therefore this boxing cannot be named by firmness, nor can it be named by softness, but is directly named by the namelessness of Taiji."

From the above four provisions one can see that the learning of Taijiquan must first destroy the hard jin originally present in people's movements, making it transform into softness; this is the period of transforming to softness. The longer this period, the more thoroughly the rigidity can be destroyed. The essential point at this time is that one must still not lose pliancy, and beneath softness advance toward a more elastic firmness and hardness. This · 50 · firmness is not the firmness of "pig iron" produced from straining and bulging effort, but an elastic firmness produced from loosening and lengthening. Because the body and limbs lengthen and constantly twist back and forth in spiral fashion, this elasticity can be produced. Therefore it can also be named "ward-off-jin firmness". The more this tautness can be kneaded into softness, the more firm and hard the inner quality can be①. Only this elastic firmness can attain the requirement of "outwardly cultivate softness, inwardly contain firmness and hardness". This transformation of firm and soft is grasped through the concealment and manifestation of spirit, essence, intent, and qi. The saying "when concealed then soft, when manifested then firm" is precisely this principle. After one's skill becomes refined, the jin can be concealed extremely deeply within, making the outward form appear extremely soft, making one feel as if one has returned again to softness, while in fact the inner quality has become even firmer. Therefore the firmness-and-softness-mutually-aiding movement from softness to firmness and from firmness to softness becomes the seventh characteristic of Taijiquan.

Book page 51

I. The Boxing of Firmness and Softness Mutually Aiding

I. The Boxing of Firmness and Softness Mutually Aiding

How to view firmness and softness in Taijiquan, and what counts as correct — this is a question that all practitioners wish to know. To answer this question, one must begin from the environment in which Taijiquan developed. The people of the Yellow River basin mostly like to practise hard-style boxing, and hence the Chen-style boxing transmitted in that region also has a tendency to develop toward firmness and hardness. But the Chen family's hereditary transmitters could still preserve the Taiji yin-yang principle and manifest the special feature of firmness and softness mutually aiding. In the Yangtze River basin, intellectuals learning Taijiquan for health occupied a very large proportion. To suit the needs of their constitutions, they gradually developed toward softness. But the Yang family's hereditary transmitters likewise still preserved the style of Taijiquan as "firmness concealed within softness, a needle hidden in cotton". In the various styles of Taijiquan popular today, viewed from the organisation of the frame, they are broadly the same, but viewed from firmness-softness and speed-slowness, each has its own special features. Therefore those generally learning Taiji

  • ① Like the spring of a clock: it has the softest elastic firmness, and is also the firmness of the most solid quality.

· 51 · each boxer may learn what he loves according to his own needs. As for the saying of "pure softness without firmness" or "pure firmness without softness", no martial art whatsoever possesses it. Even in the so-called hard-style boxing, within it there is still both firmness and softness. How much more so Taijiquan, which is a boxing art that produces from yin and yang aiding each other a whole series of mutually aiding yet mutually opposed special features. Therefore the so-called "soft-art Taijiquan" or "hard-art Taijiquan" does not exist.

Book page 52

II. The Period of Seeking Softness and Destroying Rigidity

II. The Period of Seeking Softness and Destroying Rigidity

Whatever a person may be, whether or not he has practised martial arts or other sports, in his daily life he must often have carried heavy objects and used strength. Thus everyone's movements inevitably carry rigid bulging effort. If one wishes to learn the movements of Taijiquan well, then toward these original bulging efforts one must, with the drive of "temper a hundred times into steel; what hardness can it not break?", remove them — this is the initial requirement of practising Taijiquan.

In this period one should strive for softness, and must in the "hammering a thousand times and refining a hundred times" process of walking the frame transform the rigid jin inherent in people's movements into soft jin and cultivate this habit of softness. This is the period of destroying the original rigidity and establishing a new softness. The special feature of this period is to strive for softness with all one's might, moving slowly under the principle of using not the slightest force. The less force one uses at this time, the more easily one discovers the defects in one's movements, and the more quickly one can destroy the rigid jin in one's movements. Therefore one may say this is the best "steel-smelting furnace", able to practise the movement until the segments are softly strung together.

III. The Period of Practising Softness into Firmness

The requirement of the above period of seeking softness and destroying rigidity is the initial requirement for transforming hardness into softness. The present period is the period of transforming softness into firmness. In this period one must first make clear what kind of firmness in nature this firmness is, and how one can move softness to become firmness. The boxing manual says that in practising the form one must "with intent seek softness, without intention become firm"; therefore the movement must not use force, and requires the whole body to loosen. This kind of "looseness"

· 52 · is a conscious looseness, but not a looseness that is silent and without intent, and at the same time it has nothing in common with straining and bulging effort. What is called "looseness" means attaining looseness by lengthening the body and limbs, and by the lengthening of the loosening making the body and limbs produce elasticity. When the elasticity is strengthened, it becomes ward-off jin, and ward-off jin is precisely the spring jin required by Taijiquan. The strengthening of this spring jin is the firmness required by Taijiquan.

Now that the nature of firmness is made clear, let us speak further of how one can move softness to become firmness. The strengthening of firm rigidity is realized by the continuity of the inner qi. The raising of the quality of firm rigidity is realized by twisting the reeling-silk jin back and forth to strengthen the toughness of the elasticity. Therefore movement like reeling silk and the lengthening of the body and limbs become the key to attaining both the softest and the firmest. This is what the boxing manual says: "Constantly seek softness on the outside, and over time one naturally obtains firmness and hardness within"; "it is not intentional firmness and hardness, but truly intentional softness." Taijiquan is thus transformed from softness into firmness and hardness, and only this firmness and hardness transformed from softness can attain the proficient realm of sudden softness and sudden firmness, of both soft and firm.

Book page 53

IV. The Transformation of Firm and Soft

IV. The Transformation of Firm and Soft

The transformation of firm and soft, in terms of spirit and qi, is manifested through concealment and manifestation — concealed then soft, manifested then firm; in terms of posture, it is through opening and closing — in the course of moving jin it manifests as softness, and when the movement reaches its landing point it manifests as firmness. Because of the coordination of the concealment and manifestation of spirit and qi with the opening and closing of the jin-posture, firm and soft can be fully manifested. The landing point is the point where the movement reaches its end, and is where spirit manifests and qi gathers; therefore at this time and place to use the firm method may be called hitting the mark exactly. Apart from this, in all processes of opening-closing and conversion, because they are all processes of spirit-and-qi drumming-and-surging and of round living conversion and change, at these times it is fitting to use the soft method. To sum up, every boxing form movement has opening and closing, and every process of opening and closing has the landing point of the movement; at the landing point one uses firm jin, and everywhere else uses soft jin, so as to achieve firmness and softness mutually aiding. This is the correct place for applying firmness and softness mutually aiding, and is a principle that must be observed · 53 · and is also the foundation for practising out the eight categories of jin. In this respect, one may follow the account in Chen Naizhou's boxing manual, in the "Discussion of Firmness and Softness Mutually Aiding", which sums up the transformation of firm and soft into five points, for reference.

(1) If one uses purely the firm method, then the qi spreads over the whole body, hauling and pulling are not smooth, and on reaching the landing point one certainly cannot manifest firmness and hardness.

(2) If one uses purely the soft method, then the qi scatters and does not gather, has no place of return, and on reaching the landing point one likewise cannot manifest firmness and hardness.

(3) If one should be firm but uses soft, then the qi that should gather does not gather; if one should be soft but uses firm, then the qi that should scatter does not scatter — in neither case does one obtain the wondrous function of firmness and softness mutually aiding.

(4) Therefore one who is good at using firm and soft: on reaching the landing point uses firmness, like a dragonfly touching the water, rising the instant it touches — this is the correct image of manifesting the firm point. In all movement and conversion one uses softness, like a cartwheel rotating and rolling on without stop — this is the correct image of manifesting the soft point.

(5) Only thus does one obtain the wondrous function of firmness and softness mutually aiding, and only thus can one remove the defects of qi-deficient insubstantiality and of clogged-and-unsmooth sluggishness.

Book page 54

V. The Grasping of Firmness and Softness Mutually Aiding

V. The Grasping of Firmness and Softness Mutually Aiding

(1) Strive for softness — when first learning to walk the frame, one is mainly learning the various postures. Through learning these different postures, one first transforms away the rigid jin originally on the body, and this rigid jin everyone possesses. Therefore at this stage one should spare no effort in striving for softness as much as possible; for those who previously learned hard-style boxing and later switched to learning Taijiquan, this is all the more important.

(2) Strive to lengthen the body and limbs, in order to produce elastic firmness — after practising thus very softly and very slowly for one or two years, if the rigidity in one's movements has already been wholly removed and one has reached the degree of pliancy, and has already formed this habit, one can then shift to the next step of practice. At this time, one should first, in intent, have the intention of lengthening every place on the whole body, and in posture and movement · 54 · vigorously carry out the special practice of lengthening according to the boxing manual's provisions (such as hollowing the crown and holding up the top jin, sinking the qi to the cinnabar field, containing the chest and drawing up the back, and so on), thereby making intent and body-and-limbs, in close coordination, single-mindedly and whole-spiritually lengthen, in order to obtain elastic firmness. When first learning the form, for the various provisions of lengthening, such as containing the chest and drawing up the back, it is enough merely to use intent; but at this stage, one should carry it out jointly in intent and in body-and-limbs, because by now lengthening will no longer give rise to the contrary morbid sign of bulging effort.

图 16
Diagram of firmness and softness mutually aiding (the diagram marks the soft-moving line (round line), the movement's landing point, the firm point (square point), and square-and-round generating each other)

(3) Do well "softness moves the qi, firmness lands the point" — after the whole-body lengthening has met the requirement, one can further, at the landing point of each opening and closing, in conjunction with the outward manifestation of spirit and qi, form the square point, manifesting the jin categories of the four cardinal and four corner directions; this is the practice of the square within Taijiquan's "square and round generating each other". At the square point one must manifest extremely firm firmness (that is, one must make the body and limbs taut to the extreme and long), and after the firmness has passed, one requires that throughout the entire process of movement one manifest extremely soft moving of qi. The whole round of the frame should be carried out under such a condition of firmness and softness mutually aiding. Therefore when practising the form one should firmly remember the six-word essential: "softness moves the qi, firmness lands the point".

(4) The application of firm and soft and "vigorous spirit and bearing" — the application of firm and soft must be combined with the application of intent, spirit-and-qi, and breathing; that is, on the basis of "vigorous spirit and bearing"

· 55 · one coordinates the use of deep and long exhalation to make the body and limbs sink and lengthen, thereby strengthening elasticity and becoming elastic firmness (as in issuing jin); on the basis of quiet intent and gathered qi, one makes the muscles of the limbs loosen along with it, thereby forming a lively and unclogged softness, and from softness changing in ten thousand ways. Both of these are physiologically a kind of natural phenomenon.

In short, the firmness of Taijiquan is not the firmness of bulging effort, and the softness of Taijiquan is not an elasticity-less softness; rather, "vigorous spirit and bearing" manifested outwardly becomes firmness, and quiet intent and gathered qi concealed inwardly becomes softness. When intent moves, spirit and qi follow; as spirit and qi conceal and manifest, so firm and soft transform. Therefore in practising one round of the frame, spirit and qi should conceal and manifest suddenly, intent should unceasingly direct, and spirit and qi should also unceasingly conceal, manifest, and drum-and-surge; only thus can the muscles unceasingly transform firm and soft. This is an important path for grasping and practising the transformation of firm and soft.

In order conveniently to grasp the seventh characteristic, its essentials are summarized as follows.

(1) In the initial period one must transform away the original rigid jin, and the softer the better; the longer this period the better too, generally requiring one or two years.

(2) After the whole body has been practised to pliancy, one can then proceed to concretely practise the lengthening of the whole body, in order to practise firm jin.

(3) Moving the qi uses softness, the landing point uses firmness — this is Taijiquan's dividing line between firm and soft.

(4) Intent combined with the sudden concealment and manifestation of spirit and qi and with breathing is Taijiquan's rule for the transformation of firm and soft.

(5) Firmness and softness alike attaining a high level is the standard for the title of Taijiquan marvellous hand①.

  • ① According to Chen Xin's "General Discussion and Elucidation": "Pure yin without yang is the soft hand, pure yang without yin is the hard hand; one yin and nine yang is the root-headed stick, two yin and eight yang is the scattered hand; three yin and seven yang still feels hard, four yin and six yang is akin to a good hand; only five yin together with five yang, yin and yang without bias, is called the marvellous hand; the marvellous hand in one movement is one Taiji, and when the traces are fully transformed it returns to nothingness." This is the Chen style's standard for the softness-firmness degree of Taijiquan. Because Chenjiagou lies in the Yellow River's slope, where many practise hard-style boxing, and hence people fear that they will be tempered by their environment into gradually tending to hardness, there are the names hard hand, scattered hand, good hand, marvellous hand, to serve as the standard limiting practitioners from tending to hardness.

Eighth Characteristic: The Movement of Alternating Fast and Slow, from Slow to Fast and from Fast to Slow

Eighth Characteristic: The Movement of Alternating Fast and Slow, from Slow to Fast and from Fast to Slow

The boxing manual lays down①:

(1) "When the opponent moves urgently then respond urgently, when he moves slowly then follow slowly";

(2) "When he does not move, I do not move; when he moves slightly, I move first";

(3) "When first learning one should be slow, but slow must not become idiotic; after practice one becomes fast, but fast must not become chaotic";

(4) "The form resists the five peaks, the posture presses the three summits; from slowness enter swiftness, from shallow enter deep".

From the above four provisions one can see that when first practising the Taijiquan routine (one round of the frame), the movements should be as slow as possible, and the time may be drawn out. Only when the movements are slowed is there opportunity to make corrections, and only thus can one examine the places that are not smooth. But slowness must not go so far that the face shows idiocy; this is the limit of slowness. Later, as one's proficiency increases, one may gradually speed up, shortening the time needed to walk one round of the frame. But in turning from slow to fast there must likewise be a limit, namely that although fast, the movements must still be steady, still be able to manifest the categories of jin, and must not give rise to floating and drifting or chaotic phenomena. This refers to the length of time needed to practise one round of the frame. On this premise of being able both to be slow and to be fast, when applying it to each boxing form one must unify this pair of opposites, fast and slow, into

  • ① In the boxing manual, the meaning of fast and slow has two contents:

The first meaning refers to the length of time needed to practise one round of the frame. If A takes twelve minutes to practise one round of the frame and B takes fifteen minutes, then we say "A is fast and B is slow".

The second meaning refers to the speed of movement within each boxing form. It is slow at the conversion, gradually quickens after passing the conversion, is fastest when carried to the landing point, and after issuing returns again to slowness.

Among the four lines of principle quoted here, the first two refer to the second meaning, and the latter two to the first meaning. This is a question that must be distinguished clearly when learning.

· 57 · a single boxing form: that is, at the conversion it must be slow, after passing the conversion it gradually quickens, it is fastest when carried to the landing point, and afterward slows again, and so on in a cycle. (As in Figure 17.) Therefore every boxing form of Taijiquan must undergo the training of being able both to be slow and to be fast; only thus can one, in pushing hands, "when he moves slightly, I move first" and "when he moves urgently then respond urgently, when he moves slowly then follow slowly", creating conditions favourable to oneself, and can attain the unity of alternating fast and slow.

Therefore the movement of alternating fast and slow, from slow to fast and from fast to slow, becomes the eighth characteristic of Taijiquan.

I. The Development Sequence of Fast and Slow

I. The Development Sequence of Fast and Slow

At the initial stage of learning Taijiquan, one must absolutely not be fast, and must strive for slowness with all one's might, the slower the better. Because slowness allows one to carefully ponder the correctness of the postures, proceeding from coarse to fine, and there is ample time to examine the ins and outs of every movement; thus the postures are easily corrected, and at the conversion one can examine whether it is smooth. But slowness is not to be slow without limit; generally after one or two years of learning, imitating, checking, and correcting, it will do. On this point one must have a correct notion when first learning. This is the period of seeking only correctness of posture, not distinctness of jin categories.

The slowness of this period must further have a condition, namely that the slowness must be sought on the premise of raising the spirit and not letting the spirit scatter. If in the movements one is so slow that in spirit and qi one manifests dullness and rigidity, and in action manifests sluggishness and immobility, then this is contrary to the requirement of Taijiquan's intent-and-qi movement. Therefore slowness must be sought under the drumming-and-surging of spirit and qi and the nimble conversion of intent and qi; this is Taijiquan's standard for slowness. For this reason, when first learning one must absolutely not contract this habit of sluggish intent and dull spirit, causing difficulties for later improvement.

Later, as one's proficiency increases, one may gradually quicken the speed; but fast must not be chaotic — this is the period of training the categories of jin. Finally, after one's skill has become refined, the boxing forms may develop from extension to compactness, so that the speed of movement gradually slows again, while at the conversion · 58 · its angular velocity is even faster. This is the three-layer skill of first slow, then fast, then again slow, and is also the three stages of the development of fast and slow.

Book page 59

II. The Time and Conditions for Turning from Slow to Fast

II. The Time and Conditions for Turning from Slow to Fast

At what time and under what conditions is it most suitable to turn from slow to fast? To answer this question, one must first clarify the two standards for turning from slow to fast.

(1) Movement steady — within the whole round of the frame, even if one moves somewhat faster than before, one still must not change the original steadiness of the movement; this is correct speeding up. If one cannot, and floating and drifting appear, then it shows the movement has been speeded up too much, and one should at once slow down somewhat. Under the guidance of this standard, one can gradually speed up as proficiency increases.

(2) Being able to manifest the categories of jin — Taijiquan is composed of the eight gates and five steps. In moving jin one should fully manifest one of the eight jins (such as the four cardinal's ward-off, roll-back, press, push, or the four corners' pluck, rend, elbow, shoulder). If the movement is too fast, it slips past in a single turn, and it is not easy to manifest the required category of jin. Therefore if one feels it is very hard for one to manifest the category of jin again, it shows the movement has already been speeded up too much, and one should slow down somewhat. This is also a standard for turning from slow to fast①.

The above two points are the two standards for turning from slow to fast. With these two standards, one can be guided correctly to grasp the time and conditions for turning from slow to fast, making the speed of movement turn from slow to fast just to the right degree. The fast referred to here does not mean changing all the movements of Taijiquan into fast movements, but rather that in the opening and closing of every boxing form, at the conversions and foldings and pilings, one must manifest, in a manner of relaxed-yet-not-relaxed and about-to-extend-yet-not-extended, the lingering attach-

  • ① However much one speeds up, in order to manifest steadiness and the categories of jin, the first route's thirteen-posture frame is at fastest no more than eight or nine minutes. This was the speed at which teacher Yang Chengfu publicly performed Taijiquan at the annual meeting of the Nanjing Physical Education Research Society in 1914.

· 59 · ment and vermicular soft slow movement. Therefore the so-called fastness is manifested only in the process of turning from round to square. (As in Figure 17.) This accelerated movement is the foundation from which the eight categories of jin arise; without this angular acceleration, one cannot manifest the categories of jin of the four cardinal and four corner directions, nor can one suit the requirement of "when he moves urgently then respond urgently". The issuing jin of Taijiquan is realized precisely by using this accelerating process: under the condition of closing concealed within opening and with the inner jin curved-stored, when one reaches near the target object, one suddenly shakes and issues like a bowstring released from its catch, sending the inner jin out from within a short distance. Martial artists call this "inch jin"①.
