· 180 · Chen-Style Taijiquan, Second Routine The "Second Routine" of Chen-style Taijiquan is the second set of forms, commonly called the "Second Set" and also known as "Cannon Fist" . The Second Set runs from the start all the way to the first Single Whip: that is, from the Preparatory Posture, Step-Up Buddha's Warrior Attendant Pounds the Mortar, Lazy Tying the Robe, Six Sealing and Four Closing, through to Single Whip — these five movements are exactly the same as in the First Routine. These five movements are repeated first so that the body performs several soft postures to stretch the sinews and bones, adapting it for the demands of the Second Set. Therefore, the movement descriptions of the Second Routine in this chapter begin after the first Single Whip (chest facing south). The description of the four postures before Single Whip is given in full under the First Routine and is not repeated here. For convenience of exposition, figures 1–26 and their descriptions from the First Routine diagram are not repeated in the Second Routine's diagrams; of these, figure 26 is here listed as figure 1 of this diagram section. Explanations of the diagrams are likewise given in full under the First Routine.

Form Six　Pieh-Lan Elbow (Slanting Parry Elbow) (chest facing south)

Movement: The center of gravity shifts slightly to the right; at the same time, the right hooked hand on the right side changes into a fist with a small forward reeling, with the fist-heart facing up, and the left palm changes into a fist, reeling backward from the left downward to the front of the chest. Immediately afterward the center of gravity shifts left; as it shifts left, the left fist passes across the front of the chest and strikes leftward with a horizontal blow using the fist-eye to issue power, and the right fist strikes from right to left likewise with a horizontal blow using the fist-eye to issue power — the left fist-heart facing up, the right fist-heart facing down. (Figure 2) The center of gravity shifts right; as it shifts right, both hands — the left reeling backward, the right reeling forward — strike from left to right with horizontal blows using the fist-eyes to issue power, the left fist-heart facing down, the right fist-heart facing up. (Figure 3)

图 1
In a bow stance, the right hand holds the hooked hand in front of the body and the left palm extends forward; the opening posture of the Second Routine diagrams.

Key points:

This posture has two issuings of power, left and right, which must be performed in immediate succession. In the transition from Single Whip to the leftward issuance of power, the center of gravity must first shift slightly right, and then power is issued, in order to meet the requirement of "store first, then issue." When issuing power, the movement of the center of gravity and the power of the two fists must be as one, so that the power is whole.

Form Seven　Guard-the-Heart Punch (chest facing northeast)

图 2
Facing forward in a bow stance, both fists strike horizontally to the left; the posture as the center of gravity then shifts right for the rightward horizontal strike.
图 3
Facing forward in a bow stance, both fists strike to the right, with the right arm raised in an arc.
图 4
The right leg bends and squats, the body turns left, and the left fist is lifted to guard the chest.
图 5
Standing with feet apart, both hands drawing together before the chest.

Movement: The entire center of gravity shifts onto the right leg; the left foot lifts, the body turns left, the right foot pushes off the ground and springs up, then the left foot lands, and the right foot follows with a step to the left-front (southeast) diagonal. As the body turns, at the same time, the left fist reels backward and is slightly lifted inward, then follows the turning of the body toward in an arc reeling forward to the left-rear-lower, down to the left side of the waist, the fist-heart slanting toward the upper right; the right fist, first reeling backward then forward, follows the turning of the body from the right upward, passes the front side of the right forehead and goes left, and strikes downward at the same time as the right foot lands. (Figure 4) The left fist reels forward and is raised to the left to the height of the shoulder; the right fist reels forward and draws inward. (Figure 5) The left fist goes from the left forward, passes the outside of the right fist, downward and inward; the right fist goes from the inside outward; the two fists cross past each other before the chest; then both hands reel forward, the left fist draws inward, and the right fist thrusts forward with the back of the fist near the wrist; at the same time the center of gravity sinks. (Figure 6)

Key points:

In Taijiquan movements, whenever a circle is to be enlarged, it must first be made smaller; this is to strengthen the "ward-off" energy , so that under the condition of "qi clinging to the spine" the internal power is threaded through and reaches the root of the palm. When the two hands perform the inside-outside, left-right double backward reeling and open up before the chest, the combining energy arises — right in front, left behind; finally, like the character ∞, the two circles meet before the chest to guard the heart; at the same time the circles are gradually made smaller, forming stored power like a drawn bow, to strengthen the ward-off energy.

Form Eight　Slanting Twist-Step Walk (chest toward east, turning to southeast)

图 6
In a bow stance with the body turned sideways, the two fists cross before the chest and the right fist thrusts forward with ward-off energy.
图 7
Standing with the body turned sideways, both fists crossed and drawn in before the chest.

After the above, with the two fists guarding the chest, the two fists open into palms and perform silk-reeling — right forward, left backward — uniting before the chest. At this moment the right hand is above and the left hand below, with the right palm left, with the left palm-heart facing up. Then continue with the double division — right forward, left backward. (Figs. 7, 8, 9) Then the two hands again unite before the chest, but now the right hand has already turned downward and the left hand upward, both palm-hearts facing down. Then the right hand turns up again, the left hand turns left; at the same time the body rises, the right leg is lifted, the left leg stands alone, and the two palms hold the energy together. (Figure 10) When it next turns into issuing , the right foot is brought to the ground with a stamp and becomes full. Then the left foot takes a reeling step toward the northeast, and the right palm reels forward and sinks from front to right. At the same time the left palm reels backward, turning in an arc up to the right; when it turns to the point where the left palm opens to the left, the right palm is just then reeling forward upward to the right ear. At this moment the left leg is full — this is the rising posture. Then the right palm turns half a circle at the right ear and reels backward to release toward the right front.

图 8
Standing with the body turned sideways, the two palms dividing up and down.
图 9
Standing on one leg with the body turned sideways, the two palms spread up and down.
图 10
Standing on the left leg with the right leg lifted, both palms joined before the chest.
图 11
In a broad bow stance, the two palms divided left and right, the body upright and the posture steady.

open; at the same time, the left palm, after reeling slightly backward to the right, opens forward to the left, forming a double opening energy. At this moment the chest faces south. (Figure 11)

Key points:

In this posture, when the right foot lands, the right hand opens and the left hand closes; when the left hand turns to open to the left-outside, the right hand again turns to the right ear to close. Because of the left-close right-open and left-open right-close, the internal qi is made to spiral and sink. Finally, when completing this posture, the left and right palms simultaneously open under the double backward reeling; when they have opened to the end, they close again with a double forward reeling. In the double closing, the fingers of both hands must point upward; at the same time, the internal energy of both elbows must also combine. Then, at once, the qi sinks to the dantian, and the center of gravity simultaneously shifts to the right foot. Because of the alternation of opening and closing, together with the stamping of the foot and the rotation of looking left and right, the qi is forced to descend — this is a basic exercise for moving the energy and training the qi to sink, and also the posture in which one most easily feels the qi finally settling in the dantian.

Form Nine　Lower-the-Waist, Press-Elbow Fist (chest facing southeast)

Movement: After the two palms of the previous slanting posture have divided, the right palm on the right uses forward reeling; when it turns upward, the palm changes into a fist and is placed above the right knee. At the same time, the left palm on the left uses a small forward reeling on top and becomes a fist facing the right fist from a distance, combining energy at the upper left. The crotch sinks, forming a low round crotch; the foot changes from left-full to right-full. At this moment the chest faces south. (Figure 12)

Form Ten　Well-Barrier Straight Entry (chest facing north)

Movement: The left foot is lifted and steps out 180° to the right, turning the chest to face north. The left fist changes to a palm, and with the left foot presses down diagonally from above toward the front-lower of the chest — the energy in the root of the palm. At the same time the right fist reels forward and also changes to a palm as it sinks.

图 12
In a low horse stance, the right fist placed above the right knee and the left fist combining energy above.

turn over the palm so that its heart faces up and brings it near the left of the waist. When rotating, the waist and spine serve as the central axis. At this moment the right foot is full. (Figure 13)

图 13
Standing with the body turned sideways, both hands turning over at the sides of the waist, palm-hearts facing up.
图 14
Standing upright with feet together, both arms spread left and right, palm-hearts facing outward.

Form Eleven　Wind Sweeps the Plum Blossoms (chest facing south)

Movement: After the left hand has completed the 180° press from above downward, the right hand then takes over the left hand's plucking-freeing energy, reeling forward from below and then upward, plucking and turning 180°; when it reaches the upper right, it again turns into a backward reeling and opens. At the same time, the left hand below reels backward and divides to the lower left, forming a double opening energy. At this moment the left foot is full and serves as the central axis of rotation; the right foot, following the body's right turn, takes a cross-step to the west of the left foot. Finally the posture of figure 13 is formed. At this moment both hands have already changed into double backward reeling.

Key points:

The function of the above three postures lies mainly in the right palm of the double opening of Form Eight: supposing it has been seized and held, one therefore, at the same time as making a small forward reeling to change the palm into a fist, follows the essential energy of the pluck, turns and presses downward, twisting the body around. This is the basis for using continuity and following to seek release. In turning the body, the downward-pressing energy of the left palm and the upward-lifting energy of the right palm are used at the same time, making the left and right hands shake up and down as one, in order to achieve the aim of release. In the course of such a large body turn, one must rotate with steady energy; the method is not to permit a flat (horizontal) rotation, but rather to make the rotation go from · 186 · above downward (in the closing), and then again from below upward (in the ward-off opening), so as to achieve, within steadiness, the freeing effect of the backward reeling. This kind of silk-reeling with a large body turn most easily produces the phenomena of "defect," "concavity/convexity," and "break/continuity." Therefore, to avoid the above shortcomings, the key point is to hold the ward-off energy with the two arms connected, and at the same time to use the waist and spine as the central axis, so that one can rotate with tension, producing a rotational momentum like that of a windmill. In the course of rotation, first press and close the energy 180° to the rear-lower, to strengthen its steadiness; at the same time, without stopping, ward-off and open the energy 180° to the rear-upper, finally completing the 360° great body turn. In the use of energy types, the upper half-circle is a closing energy rotating mainly by the left hand; the lower half-circle is an opening energy rotating mainly by the right hand. In this way the internal power continuously manifests outward and reaches the back, and no longer produces such shortcomings as defect.

Form Twelve　Buddha's Warrior Attendant Pounds the Mortar (chest facing south)

Movement: When the previous posture is completed, the double opening energy of left and right backward reeling has been used. This posture changes from the opening energy of left-right double backward reeling into the closing energy of left-right double forward reeling, making the qi pour to the little fingers. At this moment the left foot is full. (Figure 15) After closing, it again changes into a double dividing energy of upward-downward backward reeling; when it reaches the end point of right-up left-down, the right palm turns and changes into a fist, then reels forward from above downward; at the same time the left palm reels backward to the front of the lower abdomen, palm-heart facing up; finally there is a closing energy that makes the right fist fall into the left palm-heart; at the same time, when the left foot is full, the right foot is lifted and stamps the ground. (Figure 16)

图 15
Standing upright with feet together, the two arms crossed before the chest, the two palms combining energy.
图 16
Standing with feet together, the right fist dropped into the left palm, the right foot lifted to stamp.

Key points:

After completing the 360° great body turn, the internal qi should be like a wheel agitating in all directions, and afterward descend into the dantian and be pounded solid — this is the main function of this posture. When it changes from the mutual opening and closing of left and right into the mutual opening and closing of above and below together with the foot stamp, the qi can be more firmly pounded solid within the dantian. This foot stamp may be light or heavy; what matters is mainly the ability to use intent and qi to send it down, and not the lightness or heaviness of the stamp itself. Therefore, besides using the sound of the stamp to test whether the power is whole or not, one must also see whether one can achieve the skill of uniting movement and stillness, so as to reach "when there is one stillness, there is nothing that is not still."

图 17
Sinking into a horse stance, the two hands facing each other above and below before the chest, palm-hearts facing each other.
图 18
In a bow stance with the body slanting, the right arm raised above the head and the left palm pressing down.

Form Thirteen　Shelter-the-Body Punch (chest facing south)

Movement: Beginning from the closing energy after the previous posture, both hands reel backward and divide downward to left and right; at the same time as the double opening, the right leg takes a half-step sideways to the right; after opening, they close again — at this time the two hands continue reeling backward from below forward and upward, and finally the left hand is placed outside the right hand, joining before the chest, forming an open hip and round crotch, with the left foot empty. (Figure 17) This is closing then opening, and opening then closing again — a tight, small opening and small closing. Then the right palm turns to the right-rear and reels backward outward, becoming a fist; the left palm reels backward to the lower left and also becomes a fist. After the double division, the right fist reels backward from below to the upper right, then passes before the top of the head, and turns back to the left. When the left fist reeling backward arrives at the left hip, · 188 · The right fist suddenly withdraws the body and returns, issuing elbow energy to the upper right; the center of gravity shifts right, the right leg turns solid, and the whole body sinks to the right accordingly, the leg likewise lowering. (Figure 18)

Key points: With the chest contained and the back pulled up, the circles are tightened and loosened by the double reverse-twining silk to strengthen the elastic resilience within the warding (peng) energy of both arms; this produces a kind of body-wrapping, ring-shaped energy-storage action. It mainly trains the right hand and the lumbar spine, changing from a large circle to a small circle in order to strengthen the stored energy (at the same time it also contains a rightward shoulder-leaning energy); finally, from a single small circle it advances to no circle at all, threading the energy through to the tip of the elbow. It is therefore a compact, briskly moving posture, requiring that under the joining of the double reverse-twining silk one continue turning with the double reverse-twining silk. In the course of the turn one must achieve a state in which the internal energy has neither defect nor interruption. Hence its key point lies in using the lumbar spine as the central axis; when the right hand begins with reverse twining and turns to the front and then makes one large reverse-twining circle, it must be expressed as joined link by link. When it then passes from reverse twining to forward twining and suddenly reverses once more to reverse twining, issuing elbow energy outward to the upper right, one must be able to see that the energy arises from the heel and takes form at the tip of the elbow.

Fourteenth Posture P'ieh-shen Ch'ui (Swinging-Body Punch) (chest faces south, turning southeast) Movement: When in the preceding posture the left fist is placed at the crotch and the right elbow energy is issued, suppose that the left fist placed at the crotch is suddenly plucked; then following the essential force of the pluck, first with a small circle of right forward-twining and left reverse-twining, the torso turns slightly to the right, the right foot becomes solid, and then immediately with the left forward-twining and right reverse-twining the back of the fist is turned over to strike back out to the left side with warding energy. At the same time, the right hand, with a small reverse twining, releases energy toward the right rear in order to maintain balance (this is a double-opening issuance of energy). But the issuance of energy must concentrate on one side; in this posture the left side is the host and the right side is the guest, so the right fist belongs to the releasing of energy while the left fist belongs to the issuing of energy. At the same time, at the moment of issuing, the right leg is solid and the chest faces southeast. (Figure 19)

图 19
Fourteenth Posture, P'ieh-shen Ch'ui: the body turns slightly right, the left fist turns over its back to strike out to the left side, the right fist releases energy toward the right rear, the chest facing southeast.

· 189 · Key points: When the left [fist] has turned to the left crotch and the left arm is again plucked, in order neither to lose nor to resist, one should adapt to the essential force of the pluck and, following the direction of the opponent's essential force, strike out to the left with energy. This is a direct and straightforward technique for seeking release. Therefore in this posture the left fist counter-strikes as the main action, but the root of the strike lies in the right fist, which rotates with forward twining at the upper right, and through it the internal energy is threaded and poured into the left arm.

Fifteenth Posture Chan-shou (Chopping Hand) (chest southeast, turning north) Movement: This posture supposes that in the strike of the preceding posture "P'ieh-shen Ch'ui" no release was obtained; then once more, following the direction of the essential force, step up with the right foot; the right hand, with forward twining, turns up from the right rear and over with the body, and joins above the left hand; at the same instant that the plucked left hand is suddenly lifted, the edge of the right palm chops down like a knife, forming the double-opening forward-cleaving posture of left high and right low, accompanied by a sinking stamp of the right foot. This is stepping up with the right foot so as to place both hands within one's own square-and-round circle; it is a technique of striking free in which two hands and one foot act simultaneously. At this moment the chest has turned to the north. (Figure 20)

图 20
Fifteenth Posture, Chan-shou: stepping up with the right foot, the right hand turns up with forward twining and then the edge of the right palm chops down, the left hand simultaneously lifting, forming a double-opening forward-cleaving posture of left high and right low, the chest turning to the north.

Key points: This is the method of releasing the plucked left hand a second time. The method most commonly used in plucking energy is the downward-pressing pluck, which forces the opponent to find it hard to follow, so that the plucked person cannot but tend toward a kneeling posture; hence he cannot but adopt a hand-leading-the-body step-up, so as to hasten the method of release in which the "right chop," the "left lift," and the "foot stamp" are all three applied together. Therefore, under the requirement that the right hand's energy be unbroken, one uses a small forward-twining rotation to step up with the right foot, bringing the plucked left hand within one's own square-and-round circle; this is the basic method of using lightness to overcome heaviness. Before stepping up and after stepping up, as well as · 190 · When chopping down, the tail gate (coccyx) must in every case be centered and upright; on no account may the downward strike cause the tail gate to topple forward.

Sixteenth Posture Fan-hua Wu-hsiu (Turning the Flower, Dancing the Sleeve) (chest north turning south, then turning northeast) Movement: Suppose the second release has still not succeeded, that is, beneath the lifting-up and chopping-down the opponent's plucking hand still cannot be chopped away; then one must, by a turning-over movement of the body, release further — that is, following the opponent's upward-resisting chop energy, suddenly leap up; the left hand, with reverse twining, lifts up and circles over the top of the head, and the body turns over. This is a great turning of the body from below upward. The inertial force of the turn is led by the left hand. At this moment the right hand also uses reverse twining from below upward to assist, and with double-opening energy the body leaps up and turns over. At the same time the left foot lifts, and brings the right foot to leap up along with it. This movement includes using the energy of both arms and the shoulder-leaning to release the plucked hand. (Fig. 21; this figure is the instant of leaping up and turning the face) Then, in the continuing top-to-bottom rotation, when the left hand on the left side passes from reverse twining to forward twining and moves downward, the left foot simultaneously lands with a foot stamp. This is an action performed by the left hand and left foot at the same time. When the left foot lands and the right foot steps forward to the right, the right palm must simultaneously pass from reverse twining at the rear-upper position to forward twining, and chop down forward with the edge of the palm (at the chop the energy is the same as the chopping energy of splitting the frame). At the same time, the left hand forms a fist and, with forward twining, strikes out to the left rear as the guest. At this moment the left foot is solid. (Fig. 22; this figure is the posture at the moment of rotating the body, landing, and giving one chop)

图 21
Sixteenth Posture, Fan-hua Wu-hsiu, the leap-up and turn of the face: the body leaps up, the left hand lifts and circles over the top of the head turning over, the right hand assists, the right foot leaps up along with the left foot.
图 22
Fan-hua Wu-hsiu, landing with one chop: the left foot lands with a foot stamp and becomes solid, the right foot steps forward, the edge of the right palm chops forward and down, the left fist strikes out with forward twining to the left rear.

· 191 · Key points: The characteristic of the preceding posture's chopping-hand release method is that both parties' arms are at the front, and the distances from the point of application of force to both parties are equal; whereas the body-turn of this posture "Fan-hua Wu-hsiu" employs the rotating action of the body method and the lumbar spine, causing the distances of the force's point of application suddenly to form a striking contrast (near to oneself, far from the opponent). That is to say, the release point is made far from the opponent and near to oneself. This relationship of one near and one far forms a change in the magnitude of the torque. After turning the body, of the two feet the left foot lands first with a foot stamp and the right foot lands slightly later; in this way the inertial force of the rotation of the waist axis is strengthened, and consequently the downward-chopping energy of the right hand is also strengthened — this is where the key to yet another method of seeking release lies. This kind of release uses the downward chop of the edge of the right palm to take over the rotational inertia of the right hand's forward-twining turn-over. At the same time, the downward chop must be loosened and elastic, for only thus can the next posture be prompted to leap up nimbly. This kind of release is also another example of using lightness to overcome heaviness, and is the concrete expression of one technique serving two purposes, that is to say, a dual use in which release conceals a strike and the strike conceals a release. Therefore this posture consists mainly in one hand releasing while the other hand chops down following the rotation.

Seventeenth Posture Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan (Covering-Hand Forearm Punch) (chest northeast, turning east) Movement: This is a posture whose main purpose is the practice of storing energy and of issuing energy; within the frame of the Second Routine, it is mostly used to link things up whenever it follows a special posture. This is the first Covering-Hand Forearm Punch of the Second Routine. It borrows the elastic energy of the chop of the preceding posture: both hands, with double forward twining, leap the body up, and the front-rear positions of the left and right legs are exchanged; then the right foot lands with a foot stamp and becomes solid, and the left foot steps forward with a lifting (ch'ien/jian) movement and becomes empty. At the same time, with double reverse twining the whole body's energy is bent and stored, and the ring-circle of both arms is made smaller to strengthen the stored energy. At this moment the left hand is above and the right hand below, the right foot is empty and the left foot is solid. (Figure 23) Then, the latter half of the section is the issuance of energy. Before issuing, the right hand first makes a small reverse-twining circle and places it at the waist, the center of the fist facing upward; at the same time the left hand relatively does reverse twining, the center of the fist facing downward — this is the left storing of energy. When the right hand is at the right waist, the right hand sinks its energy, and amid that steadiness still uses reverse twining to sud- · 192 · With the momentum of the issuance, the energy is sent forward. At this moment the center of the fist faces downward. At the same time, the left hand relatively turns to reverse twining, releasing the fist backward to draw it back, and places it at the left waist. The center of the fist faces downward. When storing energy, the right foot is solid; when issuing energy, the left foot is solid. (Figure 24)

图 23
Seventeenth Posture, Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan, storing energy: the right foot solid and the left foot empty, the left hand above and the right hand below, with double reverse twining bending and storing the energy.
图 24
Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan, issuing energy: the right fist is sent forward, the center of the fist facing downward, the left hand releases energy backward and draws back to the left waist; at the issuance the left foot is solid.

Key points: This posture is the one most frequently used (six times) in the second frame, and its key point lies in strengthening the practice of the energy of "storing energy like drawing a bow." It is led by containing the chest and pulling up the back, causing both arms to possess a joining energy shaped like the character 6. When practicing the issuance of energy, there must be the issuance energy of lifting a thing up and then bringing it down. Therefore the first half-section must be like drawing a bow to strengthen elasticity, and the second half-section must further have the twining energy of releasing an arrow deep into the target. This is the concrete expression of making the movement issue far and long. For this reason, before issuing energy there must be a sinking small circle, so that the drawn-out stored energy and the issued energy become one; one may not simply use a straight-line storing-and-issuing energy that has no drawing along with it.

Eighteenth Posture Fei-pu Niu-luan Chou (Flying Step, Twisted Phoenix Elbow) (chest east turning north, then turning south) Movement: After the issuance of energy of the preceding posture "Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan," both fists make a small reverse twining in their original position, joining energy front and rear; when the right fist with reverse twining goes forward and the left fist with reverse twining goes backward to open, the right foot is accordingly lifted, and leaps forward with a flying step, landing as solid. At the same time, with · 193 · With the right foot serving as the pivot of the turning heel, the left foot sweeps an arc past the right foot and comes to the east side of the right foot, causing the body to spin in the air through 270°. (Figure 25) This supposes that in the preceding posture "Yen-shou Kung-ch'üan," after the right hand has issued its energy, it is plucked by the opponent, and it is a posture adopted when there is no time to draw it back. The opponent is applying energy along the direction of the issuance, so one cannot but follow quickly, to adapt to the person, using a flying step to comply with and transform the energy. In the course of complying with the flying step, one naturally turns the body to the left, using the back-bending-and-leaning energy to release the plucked right hand; this is similar to the various "Jade Maiden Works the Shuttle" postures of the First Routine.

图 25
Eighteenth Posture, Fei-pu Niu-luan Chou, the body spin: with the right foot as the pivot of the turning heel, the left foot sweeps an arc past the right foot, the body spins in the air through 270°, the left fist with reverse twining trailing behind.
图 26
After the great 270° turn, the wide horse stance: both hands draw apart to form one great ring, the body sinks into a horse stance, the left foot on the left, both fists separated front and rear.

It is likewise a leaping step, but the hand method is different. (Figure 26) After the great 270° body-turn, suppose the back-bending-and-leaning energy of the great turn still cannot release the plucked right hand; then after the turn, both hands with double reverse twining unite as one, the center of the left palm presses upon the opponent's plucking hand, causing both arms to form a transverse ring, and the right elbow energy strikes forward. This is the final application of one technique to two uses: it is release and also advance-and-attack. After the turn, the right foot is solid; at the issuance of elbow energy, the left foot is solid. The Niu-luan Chou finally formed is as in Fig. 27.

图 27
Niu-luan Chou, the fixed posture: both hands with double reverse twining unite as one, the center of the left palm presses upon the opponent's plucking hand, both arms form a transverse ring, the right elbow strikes forward; after the turn the right foot is solid, and at the issuance of elbow energy the left foot is solid.

· 194 · Key points: This is the final method of using the back-bending-and-leaning energy to release the plucked right hand. Because of the rotation of the body, it can also cause the distances of the force's point of application suddenly to form a striking contrast favorable to oneself, so as to achieve overcoming heaviness with lightness; it is a posture and strike that releases without seeking to be released. At the same time, what distinguishes this posture from the preceding several is that the left palm is pressed at the right elbow, and the back and elbow are joined to strike the opponent transversely. This is a special posture that presses down the opponent's plucking forearm, fixing the opponent's plucking point so that he cannot change it, and throws the person out sideways. Therefore it is likewise one technique with two uses. Its key point lies in being able, after flying out with the step, still to land with the body established upright and centered. Most especially, one must note that after issuing, both arms must still be bent and stored with reserve, rather than extending the hands fully straight. Therefore one must use the flying step to come out in order to suit the essential energy. This is the method of final release in a whole series of release movements; that is, it is an example of the Second Frame's practice of plucking and of releasing from the pluck. Although this posture strikes forward with elbow energy, its root is still in the back-bending-and-leaning energy of the right side. For this reason, its essential requirement is that only on the basis of establishing the body upright and centered can the unity of using elbow and leaning together be obtained.

图 28
Nineteenth Posture, Yün-shou, the first segment: both hands move simultaneously to the left, the body established upright and centered, the two palms tracing arcs one front and one rear.
图 29
Yün-shou, the right-turning segment: both hands move simultaneously to the right and then to the left, the two palms tracing arcs along a circular path.

Nineteenth Posture Yün-shou (Moving Hands / Cloud Hands) (the first three, chest south) Movement: Both hands move simultaneously to the left, then simultaneously to the right, and then move to the left again, forming · 195 · These make three Moving Hands, slightly different from the Moving Hands of the First Routine. After the joining energy of the preceding posture Niu-luan Chou, the center of gravity shifts entirely to the left leg, the right foot steps up alongside, with the tip of the toe touching beside the left foot; at the same time the left palm with reverse twining moves and turns to the left, and the right fist becomes a palm and, with forward twining, moves to the left. (Figure 28) Then the center of gravity shifts right, the right foot becomes solid, and the left heel first leaves the ground and lifts; at the same time both hands, the right with reverse twining and the left with forward twining, move and turn to the right, the right palm passing before the face and the left palm passing before the abdomen. (Figure 29) Then the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left, the center of gravity gradually shifts left, the left foot becomes solid and the right foot becomes empty; at the same time both hands, the left with reverse twining and the right with forward twining, move and turn to the left, the left palm passing before the face and the right palm passing before the abdomen. (Figure 30)

图 30
Nineteenth Posture, Yün-shou, the third movement: the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left, the center of gravity shifts left, the left foot becomes solid and the right foot becomes empty, both hands with left reverse and right forward twining, the left palm passing before the face and the right palm before the abdomen, moving and turning to the left.

Key points: In this posture one must, under a smooth and gentle curved movement, perform the silk-twining transformations of left forward and right reverse, and right forward and left reverse, and must lift and lower the legs under the condition of not moving the step, fully expressing the requirement of the division of solid and empty in which hands and feet follow one another above and below; this is also the basic requirement of this posture. The Second Frame, having passed through the preceding several leaping and strenuous fist postures, can here adjust its breathing movement a little. Therefore in this figure-∞ movement of the hands, the speed of movement may be slow or fast; this is the place where the Second Frame is naturally divided into sections.

Twentieth Posture Kao T'an Ma (High Pat on Horse) (chest west) Movement: After performing the first three Moving Hands, with the left heel as the axis the body turns right, and the right heel leaves the ground; at the same time both hands, the right with reverse twining and the left with forward twining, move and turn to the right, the right palm passing before the face and the left palm passing before the abdomen; when the left palm has moved and turned to the right of the body, the center of the hand faces upward. (Figure 31) Then the right foot is lifted, and the body continues to turn right; at the same time the right palm, with forward twining, passes beneath the left palm · 196 · draws in from the side, the center of the palm facing upward, and the left hand with reverse twining pushes forward past the upper side of the right palm, the center of the palm facing outward and downward. (Figure 32)

图 31

图 34

Twenty-first Posture Yün-shou (Moving Hands) (the last three) Movement: After performing Kao T'an Ma, then both hands, with right reverse and left forward twining, turn the right hand toward the right front, while the left hand turns toward the front of the chest. At the same time as this exchange of the two hands, the whole body, with the left foot as the turning axis, rotates 90°. At the same time, the right foot lands with a foot stamp and becomes solid, and the left foot opens one step sideways to the left, touching the ground first with the heel. (Figure 33) The center of gravity shifts to the left leg. The left foot · 197 · Steady the foot; the right foot steps half a step to the left, touching the ground first with the toe. At the same time, the two hands turn: the left hand with reverse (ni) coiling and the right hand with forward (shun) coiling; the left palm passes in front of the face and the right palm passes in front of the abdomen, moving to the left. (Figure 34) Then the right foot stamps firmly, and the left foot opens half a step sideways to the left; at the same time, the two hands turn: the right hand with reverse coiling and the left hand with forward coiling; the right palm passes in front of the face and the left palm passes in front of the abdomen, moving to the right. (Figure 35)

Key points: In the second routine (form) there are the first three and the last three "moving hands" (yün shou); the first three face the chest south, the last three face the chest north. Their basic requirements and functions are the same, so they will not be repeated. Therefore this form's key points no longer discuss the moving-hands action itself, but only the turn from doing the high pat-on-horse (kao t'an ma) after raising the leg to the front, into the turn toward the back. This action requires turning the body around within a gentle curve, with unbroken silk-reeling and continuous inner strength; therefore one must make a good small circle of the left hand drawn back in front of the chest in reverse coiling. Through this reverse coiling one shifts the torso, and the torso and the silk-reeling can be changed over suspended in the air. In this way not only is the inner strength kept unbroken, but it can also be threaded through into the next action. Hence this form is also a rather difficult action for practising the threading-through of section after section.

In order to make the turn-around easier, after Chen Fa-ke came to Peking, and to popularize Chen-style taijiquan, he added two boxing forms — cloud hands (yün shou) and high pat-on-horse — into this turn. Thus there was no longer the requirement of threading through while turning sharply in the air, and it became easier to do.

Twenty-second Form: High Pat on Horse (chest north turning northwest) Action: After the right turn-palm of the previous form, when the body turns left again, the two hands first both turn forward (shun) and close together, so that the two hands cross in front of the chest and pass each other; then both turn reverse (ni) and open.

图 35
Hands moving with left reverse and right forward coiling, body turning and left foot opening half a step sideways

up. When closing, the left foot is full. (Figure 37) When opening, the right foot is full (Figure 38). This is a boxing form linking to the next, and its jin is the same as "white crane spreads its wings" in the first routine; only the hands are more evenly levelled in height, and the two legs straddle wider, so as to manifest a rounded crotch.

Key points: This is a boxing form that closes from double forward (shun) coiling and then opens from double reverse (ni) coiling; it requires that in the process of turning open after closing there be no corners, ridges or hollows, so that the silk-reeling jin is carried onto the back of the bow. At the same time, it requires that in the enlarged and expanded posture one strengthen the elastic training with section-after-section threading, so as to raise the taut (beng) jin. When closing, pay attention to the two thumbs, chiefly the left-hand fingers; when opening, pay attention to the two little fingers, chiefly the right-hand fingers.

图 36
Two hands with double forward coiling and double closing, crossed before the chest, left foot full
图 37
Double reverse coiling opening up, right foot full, rounded crotch

Twenty-third Form: Linked Pearl Cannon, part one (chest northwest turning west) Action: From the opening jin of the previous form to the closing jin of this form, it is a closing by double reverse coiling. At this time, the right hand reverse-coils to the right of the chest, palm facing outward left; the left hand reverse-coils to the front of the chest, palm facing outward right; the two hands close into one closing jin in front of the chest. At this time the left foot is full, the right foot empty. Then the two hands forward-coil and press out (peng) to the front; at the same time the right foot becomes full, and when the two hands press out and come down with double forward coiling, the left foot retreats one step and the centre of gravity immediately shifts left, sitting on the left leg as full. When the two hands sink down (t'a), the whole body forms a posture of storing jin. (Figure 38) Then the two hands again turn to double reverse press out (peng) forward and upward, rolling up and storing; the right foot becomes full. Then the two hands immediately come down again from the front, leftward and backward, with forward coiling. When the two hands sink down, the left foot again becomes full. This is to add one more store on the basis of the previous stored jin. Finally, with double reverse coiling, send out the pressing-out (peng) jin. At this time the right palm faces outward, the left palm faces downward. At the same moment as the jin is issued, the right foot advances half a step forward and the left foot follows with half a step, the heel grinding the ground with a sound. (Figs. 38, 39) This is the first "linked pearl cannon" action; this form has three linked-pearl-cannon actions in all.

图 38
Double reverse coiling issuing the pressing-out jin, right palm outward and left palm down, right foot advancing half a step
图 39
Right foot following up half a step, the heel grinding the ground with a sound

Key points: This form is suited to the taijiquan "opening-door" hand technique for entering and moving within the opponent's circle. Its characteristic is that it takes the actively rotating two hands as the boxing form for entering the circle. Its hand technique is like pushing a water mill: the left hand rotates on the inside to defend the pit of the chest, and the right hand rotates on the outside to attack forward. The two hands, thus combined inside and outside, keep using the left hand to add "ice" (material) and the right hand to turn the millstone in motion. At the same time, the two feet follow up with the "heel-following" (gen pu) step. Although one does not seek to adhere to the opponent, yet as long as some part of the rotating, attacking right arm touches a point on the opponent, that touched place can serve as the point of adhesion, and one may thereupon stick and change in ten thousand ways. This form adopts the "advance and retreat with the body" and the flexible, transforming, centred and upright body method, so that when objectively one must meet changes and make transitions, there is always leeway, and one is sufficient to support all eight directions. Its Next: since the previous form is the double opening of spread wings, this form must first roll it up and store it. This is in order to store and then issue. At the same time, in order to issue more crisply, before issuing the jin one shrinks one more small circle, to further strengthen its elasticity, and then calmly sends the jin out. When issuing the jin, although the right foot is full, yet for the sake of the centred and upright relation of "the central earth does not leave its position," the difference between the fullness of the front foot and the emptiness of the back foot is required to be slight, so that one may quickly rotate and advance forward.

Twenty-fourth Form: Linked Pearl Cannon, part two (chest west) Twenty-fifth Form: Linked Pearl Cannon, part three (chest west) Action: In doing the second and third linked pearl cannons, the right hand goes from front-above with forward coiling toward the front of the chest, and the left hand goes from left-rear-below with forward coiling to close with the right hand before the chest. At this time, sitting on the left leg, the whole body again forms a stored jin. (Figure 40) Thereafter the actions from Fig. 40 to Fig. 41 are the same as the first linked pearl cannon (that is, the same as the actions from Fig. 38 to Fig. 39).

This boxing form may, according to the practitioner's need, be done several more times in succession, or taken out for special practice; its action is the same as the previous linked pearl cannons. But in order that the whole set may return to the original spot at the end, after this form has been done several extra times, the later "white snake spits out its tongue" must likewise be done several extra times, so that the number of times the two forms are done is equal. The other key points are the same as the first linked pearl cannon.

图 40
Sitting on the left leg storing jin, right hand forward-coiling before the chest and closing with the left hand

Twenty-sixth Form: Riding the Qilin Backwards (chest west turning east) Action: After the three advancing steps of the previous linked pearl cannon, the two palms close together in a double closing; first the left palm reverse-coils and turns toward the front of the chest, the fingers of the palm erect, palm facing right. At the same time, the right palm reverse-coils turning to guard outside the left forearm; the centre of gravity moves forward, the right leg is full (Figure 42). Then the right hand reverse-coils to the right-rear-above, and the left hand reverse-coils to the left-front-below; at the same time lift the left foot, the two hands separate, and with the right foot as the pivot of rotation, turn right 180° (Figure 43), turning the body to face east; when the turn reaches the east, the body is carried around by going from opening to closing. At this time the right hand is at the lower right, palm facing down; the left hand is at the upper left, the fingers of the palm erect. At this time the left foot, having been carried around with the turning body, is still lifted. (Figure 44)

图 41
Right hand reverse-coiling to guard outside the left forearm, centre of gravity moving forward, right leg full
图 42
Right hand reverse-coiling to right-rear-above, left hand reverse-coiling to left-front-below, left foot lifted and hands separating
图 43
Turning right 180° with the right foot as axis, the body turning to face east
图 44
The body carried around from opening to closing, right hand lower right with palm down, left hand upper left with fingers erect

Key points: With the right foot as the axis, when the left foot strides over following the turning body, the upper body must still not lean forward or lean backward. Because the left foot, following the body's 180° turn to the right-rear, strides across backwards, one takes the meaning of "striding backwards (tao k'ua)" and names it "riding the qilin backwards."

Twenty-seventh Form: White Snake Spits Out Its Tongue, part one (chest east) Action: After the left foot has strided backwards across in the previous form, immediately follow with the right hand making a small circle chiefly of forward coiling to the front, striking out with the taut (beng) jin of the fingers. At the same time, the left hand behind still, with reverse coiling, coordinates with the right hand and issues together toward the left-rear. At this time the left foot steps forward half a step and lands full, and the right foot immediately follows up, grinding the ground with a sound, completing the first "white snake spits out its tongue" pressing-out and issuing. (Figure 45) This boxing form is an "opposite-step" (ao pu) action that people do not commonly have; it takes some effort before one can be thoroughly familiar with its jin, or one may take it out for special practice.

Key points: This form can likewise serve as an opening-door hand technique, as a way of entering the opponent's circle with the opposite step; both use the body to advance and retreat, and no leaning or tilting body method is allowed, to avoid the fault of being able to support only one side inside the circle. In order to be able to change flexibly lengthwise and crosswise, front and back, the division of full and empty within this boxing form is the same as in "linked pearl cannon"; it likewise requires "small empty, small full" (1), so that after entering the circle, on touching any part one obtains a smooth, adhering and sticking effect. The difference lies in that the previous linked pearl cannon is the forward step, while this "white snake spits out its tongue" is the opposite step (sometimes, to simplify it and make it easy, someone changes the second "white snake spits out its tongue" to (1) "Small empty, small full" refers to the ratio of weight distribution on the two feet: suppose the two legs bear a total of 100 catties, one leg 55 catties and the other 45 catties; thus with only a tiny movement one can quickly change full and empty over; therefore those of deep skill have a small difference between full and empty, and the externally visible circles are also small.

图 45
After the left foot strides backwards, the right hand forward-coils and strikes out the pressing jin to the front, the left foot stepping forward half a step full and the right foot following up

"covering-hand forearm punch (yen shou kung ch'ui)," and afterwards do the third "white snake spits out its tongue"; this makes it much easier to do). When practising the forward stride of the opposite step, at first it feels a little awkward, so one must practise a great deal. At the same time, this boxing form is a short-distance storing and issuing, so one must hollow the chest and raise the back, with the spinal column leading, so as to achieve section-after-section threading and the issuing of jin from the spine. This is the representative action of the whole set for issuing jin from the spine. If the curved issuing is manifested only by the two arms, it does not meet the requirement. It would be even better if one could take it out for special practice.

图 46
Right hand in front forward-coiling and storing to the front of the chest with palm facing left, left hand reverse-coiling to the left flank, centre of gravity shifted back with right foot full and left toe touching ground
图 47
Right palm forward-coiling a small circle in front and striking out with the taut jin of the fingers

Twenty-sixth Form: White Snake Spits Out Its Tongue, part two (chest east) Twenty-seventh Form: White Snake Spits Out Its Tongue, part three (chest east) Action: The stored jin of the previous "white snake spits out its tongue" was completed by the closing posture of "riding the qilin backwards" splitting and turning and then one more closing jin. But the stored jin of this "white snake spits out its tongue" is stored after the issuing jin of the "white snake spits out its tongue." This is the point of difference between the two "white snake spits out its tongue." At the start, the right hand in front forward-coils and stores to the front of the chest, palm facing left. At the same time, the left hand, on the left, reverse-coils and turns to the left flank. When storing, the two arms hold the jin together, the centre of gravity shifts back, the right foot is full, and the left toe touches the ground as empty. (Figure 46) Then the right palm, in front, chiefly forward-coiling a small circle, strikes out with the taut (beng) jin of the fingers. At the same time, the left palm behind, with reverse coiling, coordinates with the right palm and issues together. At this time the left foot steps forward half a step and lands full, the right foot immediately follows up, grinding the ground with a sound, completing the second "white snake spits out its tongue." (Figure 47) This form also, according to the practitioner's need, may be done several extra times, the same number of times as the "linked pearl cannon."

Key points: Same as the first white snake spits out its tongue.

Thirtieth Form: Turning Over the Flower at the Bottom of the Sea (chest east turning west) Action: This is a special boxing form. After the previous form's right hand has issued the pressing-out (peng) jin forward, it immediately closes with the left hand behind in a double forward coiling that crosses. After closing, with the double opening jin of right forward and left reverse, the body is turned right 180°. At this time the centre of gravity shifts onto the left foot, forming an independent posture. In the course of turning to the west, the left and right hands become fists; the right fist strikes with the back of the fist downward and backward, the fist-heart facing forward. The left fist strikes upward and backward, the fist-heart facing right. (Fig. 48. From Fig. 48 onward to the last figure, because formerly when photographing Teacher Chen Fa-ke all the photographs of the action were taken from the reverse side, in all the following figures, facing the reader is north, back to the reader is south, the left side as one faces the reader is east, and the right side as one faces the reader is west. This will not be repeated hereafter.)

Key points: This boxing form chiefly exercises the elbow joint. The left fist striking backward and upward and the right fist striking backward and downward — striking up and down — is a rarely seen issuing backward, so its key point lies in requiring that the balance of the body be maintained when issuing up and down and backward.

图 48
Left and right hands form fists, right fist striking down-backward with the back of the fist and fist-heart forward, left fist striking up-backward with fist-heart right, the body turning right 180° with the centre of gravity shifted to an independent posture on the left foot

Thirty-first Form: Covering-Hand Forearm Punch (chest west) Action: In the previous form the right leg is raised, and the two fists strike backward to the sides, one above and one below backward, the right fist, after slightly lifting up with forward coiling, sinks down again with forward coiling, the back of the fist facing down, and the right foot simultaneously stamps the ground. At the same time, the left fist, coordinating with the right fist, after slightly sinking with reverse coiling, is immediately raised; the whole body's centre of gravity is all on the one stamp of the right leg. When the right fist forward-coils until the fist-heart faces up again, and after adding a sinking jin, then it changes to reverse coiling and sends the jin out. The issuing hand must still keep some leeway, and must not be fully extended. At the same time, the left fist, raised with reverse coiling, turns once into forward coiling and issues backward as the guest (secondary), so as to maintain a double issuing with host and guest. (Figure 49)

Key points: Same as the seventeenth form, "covering-hand forearm punch."

图 49
Right fist forward-coiling, lifted and sunk, back of the fist facing down, right foot stamping the ground, left fist after reverse-coiling and sinking is raised
图 50
Right hand forward-coiling and gathering before the left shoulder, left hand reverse-coiling and extending before the chest, centre of gravity shifting right and the body turning right
图 51
The two fists separating to left and right

Thirty-second Form: Turn the Body, Six Harmonies (chest west, from north turning south) Action: From the opening of the previous form "covering-hand forearm punch," the right hand which had issued in front is gathered with forward coiling before the left shoulder; at the same time, the left hand reverse-coils and extends before the chest. At the same time the centre of gravity shifts right, and the body turns right. (Figure 50) Then, next, the two fists separate to left and right. (Figure 51) Then Shift the whole weight onto the left leg; pivoting on the left heel, lift the right foot and turn the body to the right-rear; at the same time, bring both fists together and cross them in front of the abdomen, the right fist inside, both fist-hearts facing inward. (Figure 52)

Book page 207

Form 33. Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (1)

Form 33. Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (1)

Then the right foot lands with a stomp. (Figure 53) At the same time the left foot steps sideways to the left; both hands turn to double-reverse (shun), and issue power to the left and right outer sides, slightly backward. At this moment, the fist- hearts face forward and upward, and in issuing, the left hand and left foot are dominant. This is a variation within Wrap-Whip (bian). (Figure 54)

图 52
Weight shifted onto the left leg, right foot lifted, body turning to the right-rear, both fists brought together and crossed before the abdomen, right fist inside
图 53
Right foot landing with a stomp, the posture of the body turning right
图 54
Left foot stepping sideways to the left, both hands double-reverse issuing power to the left and right outer sides, fist-hearts facing forward and up

Key points: "Hollow the chest and raise the back" means the spine is drawn taut from top to bottom. Because of the wrapping (guo) relation in this form, the back is drawn taut on all four sides—up, down, left and right. It is another special fist-form for training the emission of power from the spine, and it is also the form in the Second Routine that trains the horizontal (heng) stepping method. This is a mass-combat type of stepping. When the leg and the arm cross · 207 · This is "wrap" (guo), the storing of power in the legs. When the two legs are separated it becomes "whip" (bian), the releasing of power in the legs, which can train a person to the skill of springing sideways with a light body. The key point of this form is that before issuing, one must wrap tightly once, making the qi sink further down, and only then can power be issued crisply to left and right, displaying a firm and resilient springiness. In this way one stores and issues twice in succession. At the same time, when the two hands go from the double-reverse opening to the double-reverse closing that makes the "wrap," the whole body is tightly wrapped and the qi clings to the spine, forming a moment of fully stored power; as soon as the foot lands with a stomp, that is immediately the left-and-right issuing of power in the "whip."

Book page 208

Form 34. Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (2) (chest facing south)

Form 34. Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (2) (chest facing south)

Movement: after "turn body six harmonies" and the preceding form "Wrap-Whip Cannon" have issued to left and right, both fists turn back to double-reverse, the weight first shifts right so that the right foot becomes solid, then both fists are brought together in front of the lower abdomen and the weight shifts left; at the same time the right foot is lifted and set down to the left of the left foot, so that both fists and both feet are crossed and wrapped. This is again a "wrap." (Figure 55) At this moment the two arms are tightly wrapped, with a sinking power, and the spine must also be drawn taut. Next both fists turn to double-reverse (shun), issuing power to the left and right outer sides and slightly backward, while the left foot steps sideways to the left—this is again a "whip." (Figure 56) This form may also be repeated several times in succession as needed, the movement being the same as Left Wrap-Whip Cannon (2).

图 55
Both fists brought together in front of the lower abdomen, weight shifted left, right foot lifted and set down to the left of the left foot, both fists and both feet crossed and wrapped
图 56
Both fists turn double-reverse issuing power to the left and right outer sides, left foot stepping sideways to the left

· 208 · Key points: This is a mass-combat fist-form that is both "moving" (zou) and "attacking" (gong). Its key point is that when springing sideways and dropping down one must appear calm and not buoyant; at the same time, through the process of one wrap and one change, the power must not be broken, so as to meet the demand of mass combat where no gap can be found. Therefore, at the connecting point after the double-opening issuing of power of the first Wrap-Whip, one must make a fold (zhedie), so that the inner motive force connects gently along a curve into the second Wrap-Whip.

Book page 209

Form 35. Right Wrap-Whip Cannon (1) (chest turning from south to north)

Form 35. Right Wrap-Whip Cannon (1) (chest turning from south to north)

Movement: the double-reverse issuing of power of the second Wrap-Whip in the preceding form is a double-opening power; after opening, there is again a double-sinking power outward and down, and both fists change to double-reverse twisting and are stored up, brought together in front of the lower abdomen with the backs of the fists facing each other; at the same time, taking the left foot as the central pivot of rotation, lift the right foot, and using the double-closing power of both fists—the left arm making a small circle, the right arm making a large circle—carry the body turning 180° to the left, the left foot sweeping half a circle with the sole adhering to the ground as the body turns. (Figure 57) At this moment both fists also turn to double-reverse (shun) toward the left and right sides and issue firm power slightly backward. In issuing, the left hand and left foot are dominant, forming the first Wrap-Whip after the turn. (Figure 58)

图 57
Taking the left foot as pivot and lifting the right foot, both fists double-reverse twisting brought together before the lower abdomen with fist-backs facing each other, body carried turning 180° to the left
图 58
Both fists turning double-reverse issuing firm power to the left and right sides, left hand and left foot dominant, forming the first Wrap-Whip after the turn

Key points: It takes the left foot as the central pivot of rotation, using the stored-power "wrap" posture to turn the body · 209 · body. The left foot sweeps half a circle sideways as the body turns, and throughout this process one must still keep the body steady—this is an important condition for whether the issuing of power of the "whip" after the turn is crisp or not. The remaining key points are the same as those of the two preceding Wrap-Whips.

Form 36. Right Wrap-Whip Cannon (2) (chest facing north)

Form 36. Right Wrap-Whip Cannon (2) (chest facing north)

Movement: this fist-form is the same as the second Wrap-Whip before the turn, except that the chest has now turned to face north. (Figs. 59, 60, 61)
