"With the vast qi in the heart, operating through the whole body, though sometimes the bodily form leans and tilts, within the leaning and tilting there is naturally the qi of centered uprightness to govern it."

"As for the body method, it is originally not fixed; un-fixed yet fixed, in one's own application — horizontal and vertical, inverted, standing, sitting, lying, crouching, leaning forward and bending back, the strange and the upright generating each other, turning, leaning, sidelong, gathering and leaping all hit the mark (all having the central qi's gathering and releasing governing within); a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, hard to depict their form."

"Of the body method, whether the great body method turning the pass or the small body method passing the corner, nimbleness and agility are what is esteemed."

"One who can master this method of shifting the body has the divine mechanism of transformation within it."

"In practising boxing, the mind is the master."

"With the mind as master, the five sense organs and hundred bones none fail to obey."

"When the heavenly lord has governance, the hundred bones obey."

"Application lies in the mind — this is the true secret." "The central harmonious primordial qi follows wherever intention goes; where intention points, the whole spirit is poured in."

"Movement and stillness, slowness and urgency, revolving and turning follow the mind."

"Transformation and neutralization lie entirely within one mind."

"The four limbs operate according to the mind, and the organs and bones all joyfully comply and follow — yet all must be carried out with the upright qi of heaven and earth."

"When the heart has not a single thing, it is extremely empty and spiritual; once there is any attachment, then it is neither empty nor spiritual, · 280 · Only by upholding it with quietude, and nurturing one's sincerity until movement and stillness are both fitting, are its transformations unfathomable."

"The subtle mechanism is fundamentally issued from the heart."

"It is asked: what is the sovereign of movement? Answer: the sovereign is in the heart. When the heart wishes the left and right to alternate in movement, then the left and right hands and feet at once alternate in movement; when the heart wishes to use the silk-reeling energy to turn the circle with the grain, then the left and right hands at once use the silk-reeling energy to turn the circle with the grain; when the heart wishes to sink the elbow and press the shoulder, the elbow at once sinks, the shoulder at once presses; when the heart wishes the chest and belly to close at the front, the waist energy to plumb down, the chest-opening to be round, then the chest closes to the front, the waist energy plumbs down, the chest-opening at once becomes round—nothing fails to accord with the intent. When the heart wishes to bend both knees, both knees at once bend; the right foot moves with the right hand, the left foot moves with the left hand, and the knees with the left and right feet all follow—otherwise many flaws and entanglements arise. This is why the body and limbs cannot but obey the heart. Hence I say: the heart is the sovereign of the movement of the whole body."

"Someone asks: the general outline of the boxing has been heard and understood, yet when it comes to striking one cannot bring out the spirit and expression—why? Answer: this lies in ordinarily casting off the desire for speed. As Mencius says, one must have the matter at heart yet not force it aright; the heart must not forget, nor must it help it grow. On the ground, first cast off the breath of levity and fluster, clear the heart and lessen the desires, calm the heart and quiet the energy, and let every posture follow rule and measure. When practice is long and skill mature, then the layered twists and turns within—having passed through every difficult stage—sorrow departs and sweetness comes; wit and delight spring up abundantly, irrepressible, and within the heart there is feeling and there is scene, and of itself one brings out the spirit and expression. In sum, all this is within human power; as for transforming without deliberate mind, that lies in nurture—over long days of effortless wandering, awaiting its coming of itself, and then one attains it."

"One shred of numinous mechanism depicts the Great Harmony; it is wholly by the square inch [the heart] that changes come in plenty. When intent has run to the place beyond intent, the clear autumn water lets the Tai'e [great sword] emerge."

"Though boxing be a small art, it is all rooted in the correct principle of the Great Ultimate."

"Though boxing be a martial art, when one gains its correct way (the way of the mean—neither leaning nor tilting, neither excess nor deficiency), there is nowhere it is not fitting."

2. Opening and Closing, Substantiality and Emptiness; Breathing Comes Naturally "Opening and closing, substantiality and emptiness—this is the boxing classic."

"Take the primal energy inherent in my body and move it within my body; its bending and stretching, coming and going, gathering and releasing, seizing rolling—nothing more than one opening and one closing, one emptiness and one substantiality, that is all."

"One opening and one closing—the art of boxing is exhausted in this."

"Movement and stillness cycle—how could there be any interval! What I mean is: one movement and one stillness, one opening and one closing, suffice to exhaust the subtlety within the boxing."

"One opening and one closing, the subtlety enters the minute; above, below, and the four sides all dissolve into the mechanism of transformation. Even if the six children [the six senses] all had cunning tongues, they could scarce depict the flying snowflakes."

"Opening and closing are originally without fixity; bending and stretching—the postures are linked. The Great Ultimate divides into yin and yang; the spirit dragon transforms without fixed direction."

"Shutting and opening, hard and soft, accord with the natural; one lifting, one lowering—principle cycles."

"One opening and one closing—there is change and there is constancy, substantiality and emptiness both attained, now appearing, now hiding."

"Within opening there is closing, within closing there is opening; within emptiness there is substantiality, within substantiality there is emptiness."

"Within substantiality there is emptiness, within emptiness there is substantiality—the natural wondrous function of the Great Ultimate. Only when the result is reached does one awaken to the exquisite subtlety of this principle."

"When the whole body closes together into one piece, and the spirit and energy do not scatter, only then can the single energy flow unimpeded and guard the whole body."

"In practicing the boxing one regulates and nourishes the blood and energy, and breathing follows its own nature. ... Regulate the breath softly and continuously, hold firm and guard within, attend to the mysterious gate. ... Move ever so lightly, stop silently, and only let the intent move."

"Head upright, eyes level in gaze; shoulder joins with shoulder, elbow with elbow, hand with hand, the thigh root with the thigh root, knee with knee, foot with foot. Calm the heart and quiet the energy; on closing, above and below close together as one; the energy returns to the cinnabar field; in all closing methods use the reverse (contra) silk-reeling method."

"When opening, all opens together; when closing, all closes together." "At the moment of closing, the energy must return to the cinnabar field."

"One opening and one closing—nothing is not natural."

"Not only should one close with posture, one ought first to close with spirit."

· 282 · "He who closes, closes the spirit of the whole body, not merely closing the four limbs."

"One opening and one closing—yin and yang complete; the four limbs (two hands, two feet) earnestly stretch the joints."

"Day by day closely contemplate the diagram of the Great Ultimate; one opening and one closing are within my own body."

"The heart must be empty; when the heart is empty, the four limbs are all empty. The cinnabar field, the waist energy, and the sole of the foot must be substantial. When these three places are substantial, what is empty in the four limbs all becomes substantial—this is called empty yet substantial."

"The principle of yin and yang in heaven and earth is nothing more than waxing and waning, fullness and emptiness; hence Confucius esteemed waxing and waning, fullness and emptiness. Practicing Taiji boxing is likewise waxing and waning, fullness and emptiness. 'Xi' (waxing/breath) means to breathe, the breath of inhalation and exhalation, and also growth; hence one's child is called 'xi' (son), because it is what one begets; and because the energy is faint, it is called 'xi'. 'Xiao' means to decrease, to recede. 'Ying' means the middle is filled full. 'Xu' means the middle is void."

3. Light and Nimbly Round-Turning; the Central Energy Fills and Suffices "To be able to revere and to be able to be still—thereby one preserves the empty spirit."

"The heart and body must not be forced with energy; move ever so lightly."

"Take nimbleness of spirit and swiftness as the standard."

"Moreover, when the heart is once empty, then the whole body is empty; only when empty is it numinous, and numinous it is enough to respond to the opponent."

"He who practices the boxing keeps the hands supremely empty and supremely numinous; when anything touches them he at once knows it, and at once can respond to it according to the moment. Not only the hands—the back and the whole body are all empty and numinous."

"Coming and going, bending and stretching, like wind blowing the willow; the heavenly mechanism stirs and surges, lively and quick, with no stagnancy whatsoever."

"With the empty and numinous heart, nourish the energy that is firm within."

"As for the movement of hands and feet, it is nothing beyond one circle; there is never going straight out and straight back." "The circles drawn have upright and slanting, but all are one circle, one Great Ultimate." "Along the way, silk-reeling; move quietly without flurry."

"Feet move with the hands, turning round as if divine."

"Departing from form yet attaining the likeness—what is not the full moon? When refining is brought to its utmost, the very smallest is also a circle." "The circle is the whole body turning—not only the hands and feet; but the hands and feet are outwardly visible, so we speak of it in terms of the hands turning."

· 283 · "The smaller and smaller it becomes, until there is no circle—only then does one return to the true divine subtlety of the Great Ultimate."

"When the central energy in practicing the boxing goes forth, who can stop it!"

"Conduct it with the vast and flowing energy, and there is nowhere it is not fitting."

"When the energy of the heart is once issued, there is nothing in the sinews, vessels, bones, and joints of the whole body that does not follow; whatever is outwardly formed is all issued from within—hence it is called inner energy."

"How is inner energy issued, and how does it move? It is issued from the heart, moves through the marrow of the four limbs' bones, and fills the flesh and skin of the four limbs."

"Not stagnant, not blocked, not perverse, not departing, not leaning, not tilting—this is the central energy."

"When the central energy is filled to the full ten parts, the energy and momentum are abundant and full."

"When the boxing moves by the central energy, men then submit in heart—and thus one transforms the whole world."

"Take drawing the foot as the stop. Learners are mostly impatient of nature; before having put in the work, they first love to strike others, not knowing where the incursion reaches—so from whatever place it reaches, one draws and strikes, not bound to a fixed pattern."

"When the central energy fills and suffices, things coming are met with compliance, and nothing can go against it."

"When the boxer's hands are complete, he can level his will, and of himself there is no wayward energy."

"Only when the central energy is carried to the hand is the carrying complete."

"The big toe waits until the hand's energy has traveled to the full, then joins together with the hand as one; only at this time can one plant it firmly."

"Its energy is all issued from within the heart, enters the bone marrow, and reaches outwardly to the flesh and skin—it is one single thread of energy, not several threads; that is, the energy issued from within the heart. When one attains its central correctness, it is the central energy; to nourish it is the vast and flowing energy."

"The central energy runs through the middle of the spine."

"If you would ask the true tidings herein, you must seek it in the joints of the spine and back."

"The central energy goes up from the Baihui point and runs down through the Changqiang point, as if threaded through by a single line."

"The central energy runs through the midst of heart and kidneys, connecting upward to the crown of the head and downward reaching the Huiyin. ... When the central energy is full and substantial within, then in opening and closing, seizing and releasing, there is of itself no obstruction." "The central energy must pass slowly through the middle of the arm slowly move, and one must not be flustered or negligent, but follow the natural rule of what is so of itself and move according to nature, not allowing leaning or tilting; and so to move the heart's energy through the middle of both arms—this is the central energy."

"When its form seems to stop, its intent does not stop; gradually fill out the inner energy, and one must cause the energy to fill from the bone marrow out to the flesh and skin, and to the fingertips. When the inner energy is filled to the full ten parts, then the mechanism of the next posture moves of itself."

"In the single energy's movement there is never any pause; it is purely the vast energy flowing and turning through the whole body, a momentum that cannot be checked."

"Only rely on the whole body being empty and numinous; one thread of central energy rises with the posture."

"When two people are opposed, it is a matter of life and death; outwardly observe the other, inwardly observe oneself; know the other and know oneself, and a hundred battles yield a hundred victories—and all is governed by the central energy, never losing the way of the great central correctness."

"Move the central energy within the heart through the middle of the four limbs; this is a place that others cannot see and only I know—one must constantly apprehend it with the spirit, and in time it becomes clear of itself."

"Raise the crown energy (crown energy: the central energy of the heart. To raise, as in lifting up). Where is the crown energy? At the Baihui point; the intent must slightly hold it (holding is holding the whole body's spirit, causing it not to lean or tilt)—that is all. It must not be overdone; if overdone, then the jaw hangs upward and one stands unsteadily. This is a key of the whole body, where the central energy passes—one cannot fail to know it. The central energy runs upward to Baihui and downward through the twentieth vertebra; when this place is once opened, then above and below are all opened, the energy and vessels of the whole body all pass through, and of itself there is no fault of toppling. The two sinews behind the head are things that assist the central energy; the place between the two sinews where there is no sinew is the path of the central energy's up-and-down flow, going down the middle of the spine to the twenty-first vertebra. Even the Ren and Du vessels, front and back, are likewise all supporting my central energy.

The central energy is the hardest to name, and the path along which the central energy moves is also the hardest to name—without form or sound. Unless one has put in long practice, one cannot know it. Therefore 'not leaning and not tilting' does not refer to outward traces, but is the name for the spirit naturally attaining the center. The central energy moved in the four limbs is also merely a side-flow of this central energy—there is not another separate central energy. When this place is not tilted, then afterward the central energy in the four limbs is all untitled; although the four limbs' outward traces show many tilted postures, yet the central energy flowing in the limbs is of itself untitled. This meaning can · 285 · be apprehended with the spirit and made clear."

"The energy is not twofold: the one that is soft yet energetic is the central energy; the one that is purely hard is wayward energy. As for its function—not leaning, not tilting, neither excess nor deficiency—this is the function of the central energy, not its substance. The substance of the central energy is the upright energy of yin and yang within my heart, that which Mencius called the vast and flowing energy that is matched with righteousness and the way."

4. Silk-Reeling Movement; Loosening and Smoothing the Channels "All the channels and vessels are beneficial to the boxing."

"In practicing Taiji boxing one must understand the silk-reeling energy; silk-reeling is the method-gate for moving the central energy. Without understanding this, one does not understand the boxing."

"Taiji boxing is the silk-reeling method. Advancing silk-reeling, retreating silk-reeling, left and right silk-reeling, up and down silk-reeling, inner and outer silk-reeling, great and small silk-reeling, with-grain and against-grain silk-reeling—yet in every case it is nothing but drawing while reeling, advancing while reeling; they cannot each be their own separate movement. If each were its own separate movement, it would not be yin and yang making each other their root."

"The whole body is all reeling energy. Broadly, inner reeling and outer reeling are both issued with the movement: there is the left hand forward, right hand back; the right hand forward, left hand back, joined in one smooth harmony; there is also the left reeling inward and the right closing at the back; there is also using the reverse-back energy to close toward the back face—each according to how its posture is, moved in the natural way. Its energy is all issued from within the heart, enters the bone marrow, and reaches outwardly to the flesh and skin—it is one single thread of energy, not several threads. That is, the energy issued from within the heart: when one attains its central correctness it is the central energy; to nourish it is the vast and flowing energy."

"In the delight of this, do not sever the spirit and energy; when the spirit and energy are unbroken, the blood and vessels naturally flow and pass through."

"Between heaven and earth there is nothing that goes forth and does not return; nor has there ever been anything straight without bending."

"For things have their counterparts, and postures have their turning back—a principle unchanging through past and present." "The root of guarding life is the wondrous formula of returning the energy. He who can skillfully move the energy can then guard his life."

"One ought naturally to follow a good teacher, and also to seek out worthy friends; everywhere follow rule and measure; one thread opens the numinous clarity. One layer deepens another, layer upon layer with endless meaning; one opening links to one closing, opening and closing succeeding and inheriting each other."

"The five movements and six energies govern transformation; the martial art that gains this of itself communes with the spirit."

· 286 · "The Ren vessel arises at the Huiyin, runs upward along the inside of the belly to the Tiantu and stops at the Lianquan. The Du vessel likewise arises from the Huiyin, passes the Changqiang, runs against the grain up the spine to the Baihui, and descends to stop at the Renzhong. ... The Ren and Du of the human body, spoken of as belly and back, ... are both located in the center, and can be divided and can be joined. To divide them is to see that yin and yang never part; to join them is to see that the undifferentiated whole has no gap. ... If a person can understand the Ren and Du in order to move the energy and guard the body, ... practicing the arts of guiding and drawing, and take this as the root of (warding off illness and prolonging life). In practicing the boxing to regulate and nourish the blood and energy, breathing follows its own nature; sweep away deluded thoughts, unload all turbid energy, first establish the foundation, draw in the sight and turn back the hearing, hold the light silently, regulate the breath softly and continuously, hold firm and guard within, attend to the mysterious gate (that is, the cinnabar field). When practice is long, then in an instant fire is issued within the water, and flowers bloom in the snow; the two kidneys are hot like soup, the bladder burns like fire, and the true energy suffices of itself. The Ren and Du are like a cartwheel; the four limbs are like mountain stone. Without a thought being issued, the heavenly mechanism moves of itself. Each time one strikes a posture, move ever so lightly, stop silently, and only let the intent move—then water and fire naturally blend and fuse. ... After refining for ten years, the whole body is an undifferentiated whole, supremely empty and numinous; one does not know the body as myself, nor myself as the body; nor does one know that spirit is born of energy, that energy has its own spirit. Turning accords with the compass, bending accords with the square; without thinking one attains it, without effort one hits the center, ... not knowing why it is so yet being so; nor does one know the Ren as the Du, the Du as the Ren, nor the central energy as the central energy. When the timing and application all fit, it naturally keeps time. This speaks of the Ren and Du's rising and descending, with-grain and against-grain, assisting the central energy to accomplish its work. When the energy moves, it is born from the kidneys; when still, it still returns to the kidneys. In each exhalation and inhalation, the going out and coming in of the true energy is all here. ... In sum, though one say a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, none is better than clearing the heart and lessening the desires, nurturing one's original source, and thereby nourishing the primal energy. When the body is originally strong and robust, one's boxing will of itself surpass others by a head."

"This energy is all issued from within the heart; on the surface of thighs and arms it seems like silk reeling. Slanting reeling, with-grain and against-grain, originally have their fixity; it most repays deep and careful study. When the study of the work has truly accumulated long, in one moment it opens suddenly into Taiji boxing; every place in the human body is then the Great Ultimate, and every movement and stillness is wholly undifferentiated."

"The arm's energy is issued from the heart, moves to the shoulder, passes the elbow, and reaches the fingers—this is the with-grain silk-reeling method. From bone to flesh and skin, from shoulder to fingers, this is issuing energy. From fingers to shoulder is the reverse (against-grain) silk-reeling method; what is called entering energy is to draw it in and come, causing the opponent to draw near to me."

· 287 · "The energy of the two legs is led up from the big toes, passes the Yongquan, rises over the outer ankle, reels inward, and moves slantingly upward, passing the Zusanli, crossing the knee, passing the Xuehai, to the thigh root. The place between the two thigh roots is called the crotch, which is the Huiyin point (for the two energies facing each other have their junction there; this place is the home to which the leg energy returns. The waist energy sinks slightly downward; when it sinks to this thigh root and opens out, the crotch energy is of itself round). After moving the foot, the heel plants on the ground, and gradually the toes pass the Tonggu, Dazhong, Waifei, as well as the Yinbai, Dadun, and Lidui, and one truly and solidly plants on the ground (the toes and sole must grip the ground; the Yongquan must be empty; if not empty, the toes do not get leverage and one cannot exert force—this is 'substantial front and back, empty in the middle').

The energy of the body and limbs each moves along its own channels and vessels, without the slightest deviation."

"One going, one coming, moving one round; the energy mechanism of above and below never pauses. From ancient times the Great Ultimate has always been thus—why need one vainly seek and scheme outside the body?"

5. Above and Below Follow Each Other; Inside and Outside Join Together "The whole body must cause above and below to follow each other, and the single energy to run through."

"Inside and outside, above and below must follow; its energy cannot be opposed or reversed."

"The one who issues the command is the heart; the one who transmits the command is the hand; the one who observes the color is the eye. This is the saying of the three arrivals of heart, hand, and eye—none may be lacking."

"Above and below, hands and feet each follow; when the rear advances and turns forward, do not delay."

"Neither first nor last, meeting and sending each other fittingly; front and back, left and right, above and below and the four sides, turning and connecting with nimbleness, slow and urgent keeping pace with each other."

"However the upper hand moves, the lower body's feet move likewise; above and below follow each other and naturally keep time."

"The essential of the hand lies wholly in the palm; the fingers lead up the movement of the whole body, and the feet following the hands is especially crucial." "The feet move with the hands, turning round as if divine."

"The chest and belly in the middle move with the hands and feet; above and below the single energy runs through—when it is said to move, all move together; when it is said to stop, all stop together."

· 288 · "Strike the head and the tail moves, the spirit and energy running through; strike the tail and the head moves, the network of vessels opened; strike the center and head and tail both move—above and below and the four sides are linked like a bow."

"Inside and outside, the single energy flows and turns."

"The eight bodies (crown, crotch, heart, eye, ear, hand, foot, waist)—close them tightly, sir, you must remember; human strength moved to completion seizes the work of heaven."

"Taiji boxing has a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations; there is nowhere that is not energy. Though the postures are not equal, the energy returns to one. That which is called the one: from crown to foot, within there are the organs and bones and sinews, without there are the flesh and skin and muscle; the four limbs and hundred bones are linked and made into one. Strike it and it does not split; ram it and it does not scatter. When above wishes to move, below of itself follows; when below wishes to move, above of itself leads; when above and below move, the middle part responds; when the middle part moves, above and below harmonize. Inside and outside are linked, front and back require each other—this is what is meant by 'one thread running through it all'!"

"The heart and body must not be forced with energy; lightly keep to rule and measure, and move by following the natural momentum. Lead the elbow with the hand, lead the shoulder with the elbow; below, lead the knee with the foot, lead the thigh with the knee. The crucial point lies wholly in leading and moving with the fingers and toes. Someone asks: if the hands and feet do not use energy at all, how do they move? Answer: the energy in the hand merely leads and holds the shoulder and arm, no more; it must not be overdone, for if overdone it is not numinous. As for the feet, they are only slightly heavier than the hands."

6. Sticking and Penetrating; Posture Following Posture "The single way of boxing is ceaseless advance and retreat, with spirit and energy running through, never interrupted." "Beginners at practice should first seek the hidden response; the incoming vein and the turning of the gate—the single energy begets one another." "Upper posture and lower posture, one energy receives and continues; do not let the spirit and energy be interrupted." "Practicing the boxing lies wholly in the starting posture; once the start gains momentum, all that follows gains momentum. Even with no opponent, moving the hands in empty air, one also feels the receiving-and-continuing to gain momentum, and the mechanism and momentum are nimble and lively. Therefore I say every posture lies wholly in the joining: at the place where bone meets bone and peg meets socket, how the previous posture falls, how this posture rises up—one must carefully ponder this. And it lies wholly in this: at every fall one must think how to walk it out to the full ten parts, with no little lack. When spirit and energy already suffice and this posture seems able to stop, yet the mechanism of the next posture has already moved, and one wishes to stop yet cannot stop; for its mechanism of wishing to stop and being about to stop has already called up · 289 · the lower posture. Hence I say: the state at this time seems to stop yet does not stop (not stopping means the spirit is not yet full), and does not stop yet stops (what stops is only one thread; the lower posture at once rises)."

"In studying Taiji boxing, one should carefully ponder every posture; if one posture is not pondered, then the mechanism and inner reason of this posture remain forever dim. In particular, at the place of continuing the above and raising the below, one should especially be attentive; if one is not attentive here, then the incoming vein is not true, and the turning of the gate is not nimble either; each posture becomes its own isolated posture, and one cannot from first to last run through with the single energy. If one cannot run through with the single energy, then with the Great Harmony's primal energy one can never find the ford."

"In ordinary practice of the boxing, everything lies in the one rise and the one turn—what is called 'gaining the momentum, contend for the incoming vein; the marvel lies in the turning of the gate.' At the moment when this posture's hand is about to rise, one must first cause the hand how to receive and continue the previous posture, not letting the spirit, energy, blood, and vessels be cut off. After having received and continued, one must think how the hand gains the mechanism and gains the momentum. When the incoming vein is true and the mechanism and momentum gained, the turning of the gate is naturally nimble and lively. If one can be thus, then another day when crossing hands with a person, one can of oneself stand first on ground that is not defeated, commanding as one wills."

When each posture is about to complete, "the trace seems to stop, yet the energy does not stop; one must wait for the inner energy to slowly move to the full ten parts of sufficiency, and the mechanism of the next posture to leap and stir, before the upper posture and lower posture can be opened through to each other, with no partition in between, the single energy flowing—not only is one posture thus; from first to last in the boxing, at the end of every posture, it is all thus."

"Where bone meets bone and peg meets socket, carefully ponder it."

"The principle is refined, the method is dense; the threads of order are unravelled and analyzed."

"Layer piled on layer, twist upon turn—all are brought to their utmost."

7. Emptily Raise the Crown Energy; Sink the Energy to the Cinnabar Field "It is asked: where is the key of practicing the boxing? Answer: below the Baihui point, from the Dazhui behind the head through to the Changqiang; its place of movement is at the Ren and Du vessels."

"The Baihui point leads the whole body."

"The crown energy is the central energy rushing upward to the crown of the head. If not led, the energy collapses; if led to excess, not only is all the body's energy then above, and the soles of the feet unsteady, the fault hanging upward, but even the crown loses firmness, — being twisted and unable to turn, thereby revealing clumsiness — lies simply in holding to the middle between "as if present" and "as if absent."

"Boxing is entirely a matter of the top-head energy (ding jin). When the top-head energy is well guided, the spirit of the whole body is roused as one."

"The whole guiding principle lies in the top-head energy; thus when the top-head energy is once guided up, the spirit of the whole body is roused." "The central energy (zhong qi) of the top-head energy is a righteous energy; the moment the intention in the heart is raised, it travels to the top of the head, and the central energy naturally rises up — it is not something lifted by any object, but simply the intention working thus."

"From first to last in boxing, the top-head energy must never be lost. Once the top-head energy is lost, the four limbs seem to have nothing to attach to, and there is no spirit; therefore it must be guided upward, to serve as the guiding principle of the whole body."

"The top-head energy is guided upward; the intent is as if the top of the head were piercing the sky — one must not use energy to excess."

"When the top-head energy is guided upward, the slanting carries the upright; the hollow of the knee props open (knee opens out) and the energy closes (joins and holds), like the half-moon."

"The central energy ascends from the Baihui point above and descends through the Changqiang point below, as if threaded by a single line."

"To guide up the top-head energy — guiding the top-head energy does not mean stiffly forcing the two great tendons behind the head and between the ears; rather it is the lifting of the central energy. As if intending, as if not intending; neither light nor heavy; as if existing, as if not existing. A single spark of sudden nimble energy in the heart flows into the back of the crown — it must not be lifted too far, nor must it fall short. Lifted too far, it hangs suspended above; falling short, the energy lingers in the chest and is hard to bring down. This is the style of the top-head energy."

"The central energy runs through the midst of the heart and kidneys; it communicates upward with the top of the head and reaches downward to the Huiyin point."

"The top-head energy is guided up, the turbid energy descends, and the central energy is stored and settled into the cinnabar field (dantian)."

"In man's body the waist is the middle boundary; energy travels up and down, and the waist is the boundary between them."

"Mencius said: The will is the commander of energy; energy is the filling of the body. The heart is like a general, energy like soldiers; when the general issues one command, the officers and men all obey. The clear energy rises and travels to the hands, the turbid energy descends and travels to the feet; all energy travels to the fingertips and then stops. The cinnabar field is the resting place to which the whole body's energy returns, like the encampment of troops. The upward and downward travel of energy seems like two separate stubs, but in truth it is one energy running through."

"The Baihui point leads the whole body; one must make the clear energy rise and the turbid energy descend. How does the clear energy rise? Without calming the heart and quieting the energy, it cannot. The turbid energy must descend to the feet. Once one posture is complete, the upward [energy...] · 291 · [...] so that the clear energy of the body all returns to the cinnabar field; for once the heart's energy descends, then not one of the whole body's energies fails to descend with it."

"All the energy of the whole body that is issued outward is issued from the cinnabar field; all that is drawn inward is gathered into the cinnabar field. Yet all is governed by the heart, and everywhere one sees the air of the great harmony and primal energy." "When energy returns to the cinnabar field, the upper is empty and the lower is full; the central energy abides in the middle, and the empty spirit is contained within."

"Once the posture is complete, the heart is calm and the energy harmonious; the central energy returns to the cinnabar field."

"The energy of the cinnabar field divides into five places, yet in truth it is one energy running through; above and below it must not collapse — this is the one point. When the heart's energy leads once, the cinnabar-field energy rises: six parts reach the heart; of the remainder, one part splits into two strands, three parts rising to the left shoulder and three parts rising to the right shoulder, all threading through the seams of the shoulder bones to reach the fingertips on left and right. That which is within the bone seams is called the central energy; that which takes form in the flesh and skin is called the silk-reeling energy (chan si jin). The remaining four parts also split into two strands: two parts travel in the left leg, two parts travel in the right leg, all threading through the marrow of the bones to reach the toes on left and right.

"As for the saying that the central energy returns to the cinnabar field — one need not cling to it rigidly; it is enough to let the energy descend to the lower abdomen below the navel. If one examines it closely, the cinnabar field is not the source of energy — why then speak only of returning here? This is but a rough statement of the general sense. If one traces it to its source, the primal energy of the whole body all issues from the kidneys: when the kidney water is sufficient, energy is naturally strong. It is nourished in the stomach: when the stomach receives its nourishment, energy too is strong. It is stored in the liver: when liver energy stirs once, contrary energy arises crosswise, and energy loses its evenness. It is steeped in the heart: when the heart has no delusive thoughts, then the heart being calm, energy is naturally harmonious. The lungs govern voice, but truly it is the heart that sounds it; wherever the heart's mechanism goes, one need not sound it from the mouth — the heart understands first. It is strengthened in the gallbladder: when the gallbladder knows no fear of what lies ahead, energy likewise follows. It is transported in the spleen: this channel has much energy and little blood; hearing a sound it stirs, and stirring it transforms without ceasing — the heart stirs once and the spleen stirs at once. It is aided by the large intestine, which has much energy and little blood and is the officer of transmission; and further assisted by the small intestine, which lies above the front of the navel and clings behind to the spine, where dregs and impurities do not remain — turbid energy departs and clear energy arrives. The above channels all benefit boxing, and so they are mentioned. If one speaks only of the kidneys: the kidneys are the officers of strength, from which skill and dexterity emerge; this channel has little blood and much energy, stores essence in the will, is the lodging of spirit, the root of nature and life. The kidneys are two in number, each with two [ducts]: one ties to the heart, one communicates upward to the brain. The place where energy is generated truly begins here, and its final return must come back to here. As for the gate of life (mingmen), it is truly the gate through which the energy between the two kidneys comes and goes; hence it is called the gate of [...] · 292 · [...] gate."

"The life pulse is the kidneys, and it is whence the central energy comes. When moving it goes out, when still it enters. Now fixed, now not fixed — meaning that since the postures change unceasingly in time, the changes of the two energies of yin and yang are likewise not fixed." "To go out from the kidneys and enter the kidneys is the true formula."

"Cross-Tiger posture, settled form: above the waist, at the back, the Pohu and Gaohuang points turn forward toward the ribs to close; at the front of the chest, the first row on the left and right ribs — Yuanye and Dabao — belong to the triple burner; the second row — Zhejin and Riyue — also belongs to the lesser yang and triple burner; the third row — Yunmen, Zhongfu, Shidou, Xiongxiang — belongs to the lungs and spleen; the fourth row — Jueyin, Qimen, Tianchi — belongs to the liver and gallbladder; the fifth row — the yang brightness large intestine's Quepen, Qihu, Liangmen, Guanmen — belongs to the stomach and intestines; the sixth row — the lesser yin's Yufu, Shencang, Youmen, Tonggu — belongs to the heart and kidneys; and the middle row — Huagai, Zigong, Yutang, Danzhong, Zhongting, Jiuwei.

On the left and right ribs, from Yuanye and Dabao down to Youmen and Tonggu on both sides, all close toward Yutang and Danzhong; the left and right ribs each respond to one another — this is the form of the left and right ribs above the waist.

Below the waist, on the left and right, Qichong and Weidao all close toward Qihai, Guanyuan and Zhongji — this is the form of the left and right soft parts below the ribs."

"What is called the flashing-through-the-back (shan tong bei)? The central energy descends from the heart past the navel to the cinnabar field, then from the cinnabar field reverses along the conception vessel (ren mai) upward past the navel, past Shangwan, Huagai, Tiantu, Lianquan to Chengjiang (the lower lip); the governing vessel (du mai) catches it and reverses up Shuigou, Renzhong, Suliao (the tip of the nose), past Shenting, Shangxing, Xinhui, Qianding to Baihui, then descends past Houding, Qiangmen, Naohu, Fengfu, Yamen, Dazhui, Taodao, Shenzhu, Shendao, Lingtai, Zhiyang, Jinsuo, Jizhong, Xuanshu, Mingmen, Yangguan, Yaoshu, down to Changqiang (all are the points of the spine and back), and further to Huiyin, where it ends (this is the starting point of the two vessels at the lower end, the conception vessel in front and the governing vessel behind). The central energy descends from Baihui through Changqiang and Huiyin — this is called penetrating the back. 'Flashing' (shan): it is as when a man embraces you about the back of the waist; the front of the waist bends forward with a sudden jerk, head and shoulders drop down once, while the Changqiang and Huantiao behind (that is, the outer bone of the thigh) use force to pry up his lower belly, and with one upward fling his hands open of themselves, and he flashes headlong over before the front from above the tongue, falling supine before me. This is called flashing through [...] · 293 · [...] the back."

"How is the back penetrated? When the head and shoulders drop down, the buttocks fling up, and so the governing vessel reverses upward from the Changqiang point through to Baihui and on to Renzhong, and the conception vessel catches it and descends to the cinnabar field — this is the first circuit, leading yang into yin. The right hand rises from the upper arm; the conception vessel then reverses from the cinnabar field upward to the Chengjiang point; the right hand turns back with the body, the hand comes down, the governing vessel reverses from Renzhong past the crown of the head and the back of the crown, and travels down along the Dazhui and back to Changqiang — this is another circuit, from yin clinging to yang. When the right foot retreats to behind the left foot, and the right hand rises from below to above, then the governing vessel again reverses upward from Changqiang and has already reached the crown of the head at Baihui. Thus the governing vessel has traveled upward more than half a circuit; when the succeeding posture, the Shooting-Hand Fist, closes and holds, then the governing vessel goes down from Baihui to Renzhong point, and the conception vessel goes down from Chengjiang to the cinnabar field — this is the third circuit. By the one posture of penetrating-the-back, the governing vessel travels up and down three times across the back — this is called penetrating the back.

The right hand from head to upper arm is the forward silk-reeling method; from the upper arm rising, turning the body over with the hand coming down, then rising from below to above at the back, on to the succeeding posture of Shooting-Hand Fist — all are the reverse silk-reeling method."

"Shooting-Hand Fist posture: in this posture the right foot presses backward with force; the force reverses upward from the back press, reaching the crotch, then rises past Yishe, Hunmen, Shentang, Gaohuang, Pohu, to Jianyu; then from Jianyu it descends into Xiaohai, splits into Shousanli, descends to Hegu (second finger), Zhongzhu (fourth finger), Wangu (little finger), and on to the third joint of the fourth finger. The force of the right foot uses the reverse silk-reeling method: from below it reverses and reels upward to Huiyin, slants into Yishe, straight to Jianyu, and again uses the reverse silk-reeling method to reel to the fist head, the back of the hand facing upward — this is the closing force. The governing vessel reverses upward, from Changqiang up past Baihui, down to Renzhong; the conception vessel catches it at Chengjiang and descends into the cinnabar field, turning one circuit front and back, to assist the force of the right fist. Moreover the guidance of the top-head energy also depends entirely on this governing vessel. The right knee and right [leg] close and hold inward. Within the chest one must be empty; only when empty is one nimble, and the force closes forward. When the foot's force goes down and the buttocks turn upward, then the front — Qihai, the cinnabar field and the crotch — naturally close and hold the force forward. If the crotch does not close, then the lower body and the soles of the feet are both unsteady; if one is not empty, then turning left and right is not nimble. Therefore one must close and hold the force forward, and at the same time keep it empty and round.

· 294 · In the Shooting-Hand Fist, the force of the five organs and hundred bones all gathers in the fist.

He who shoots the hand easily covets forward; he does not know that if the forward coveting goes too far, not only do the left and right easily lift up, but the turning left and right is not nimble and one easily loses. Therefore it is better to fall short by one or two parts, and never to cross the boundary by a hair — this is what is meant by "the force of a strong crossbow at its last, unable to pierce even Lu's thin silk"; it is the fault of going too far. Those who shoot the fist should take warning."

8. Contain the chest and raise the back, sink the shoulders and drop the elbows "The chest must close and hold the force, and must also be empty."

"The chest must be empty and contained, like a sounding stone (qing)."

"The chest is as if bowing forward with a slight bend, encompassing and containing on all sides."

"The middle chest and belly, from the Tiantu point down to below the navel at Yinjiao, Qihai, Shimen, Guanyuan, are like a bent sounding stone and the form of bowing — this is what is called containing the chest, and this is closing and holding the force; it must be empty."

"Calm the heart and quiet the energy; do not let crosswise energy fill and block the chest."

"The chest must be reserved and contained; energy descends to the cinnabar field, and no crosswise energy lingers above."

"The crosswise energy of the chest and diaphragm is unloaded to the soles of the feet; if that cannot be, it should at least be unloaded to the cinnabar field."

"Open and loosen the chest: once the chest is loose, the whole body is at ease. One must not be intentional, nor must one be unintentional. From Huagai to Shimen one must emptily contain; one must not let crosswise energy run crosswise in the chest."

"The chest also turns circles following the hand."

"(White Goose Spreads Wings posture) The force in the chest likewise follows the right hand and the left hand — first from right going down, then left going up to the right, circling one great circle."

"The inner force in the chest is like the great-harmony primal energy turning circles."

"The great-harmony primal energy moves within the chest; each movement and each stillness accord with light and heavy."

"In boxing, all movement is led by the hands; all turning of the joints lies in loosening the shoulders. When practice is long, the bone seams of the shoulders open of themselves — it cannot be forced. If the left and right shoulders do not loosen and sink, then the turning of the joints is not nimble. Moreover, loosening the shoulder is not drooping the shoulder; when the bone joints open, the shoulders naturally sink and loosen."

"The shoulders sink down; they must not be held up."

"The mechanism of turning circles lies entirely in the shoulders; therefore the bone seams in the shoulders should be made to open and stretch."

· 295 · "The arm is as if hung upon the shoulder."

"The Jianyu, Jianjing, Futu points are all loosened and sunk."

"The bone seams at the head of the shoulder and upper arm must open. At first they are not open; one must not force them open. Before the practice has reached the point, when they open of themselves, if in the heart one says they are already open, in the end they are not open; one must toil bitterly for many days, and then they naturally can open — only then does it count as open. Once this place opens, then the coming and going, bending and stretching of the whole arm is like wind blowing the willow; the heavenly mechanism stirs and moves, lively and brimming with no sluggish mechanism at all — all depends on this. This is the pivot of the upper arm, where nimbleness hinges; one cannot be unaware of it."

"The two shoulders must always be loosened and sunk. If one sees them float up, immediately loosen and sink them; yet if they cannot but float up, let them float; when the floating is done, immediately loosen. If not loosened, the whole arm's turning is not nimble. Therefore float when it should float, loosen when it should loosen. When each posture is done, the chest closes forward, and the two shoulders respond to one another. This is the form of the two shoulders."

"Bow the shoulder and one lean breaks the bronze wall."

"The two elbows should sink down; if they do not sink, the shoulders rise, and it is unfit for use."

"The elbows' tips point downward... the knees and the elbows' tips face one another above and below."

"The elbows, whether front and back, left and right, above and below, must respond and close and hold the force."

9. Transport softness into hardness; hardness and softness aid one another "In boxing the nose is the middle boundary; the left hand governs the left half of the body, the right hand governs the right half, and each foot moves with its own hand. The heart and body must not use energy; move lightly, leading the elbow with the hand, leading the arm with the elbow. The energy in the hand should only lead up the hand and the arm, no more; if it goes beyond, it errs into stiffness. However the upper body's hands move, the lower body follows; above and below accompany one another, and the middle naturally all follows — this is one energy running through. The crotch force must be open and empty; once the crotch opens, then the heart's energy is roused."

"The skin, flesh, bones and joints — everywhere open and stretched."

"To be hard, first be soft; to lift up, first press down."

"The people of the world do not know, and all take (tai chi chuan) to be a soft art; they little realize that from the time one begins to practice, through a thousand hammerings and a hundred refinements (refining this body a hundred times into an iron man), hardness returns into softness, and softness reaches the utmost [...] · 296 · [...] hardness — hardness and softness leave no trace to be seen. But viewed from its outside, it seems like softness, and so it is named by softness; yet how could this be so? Moreover, 'soft' is only said in contrast to 'hard.' This art cannot be called soft, nor can it be called hard; it can only be named tai chi (the supreme ultimate). Tai chi means hardness and softness both arriving, blended without trace. Its achievement is much, and so its completion is hard."

"Yin and yang are each the root of the other; they cannot be divided into two stubs."

"To overcome hardness is easy; to overcome softness is hard."

"Softness can overcome hardness; to advance by retreating is the way of Kun. Kun mates with Qian; Qian is hardness. Kun is utterly soft, yet in moving it is hard. This boxing appears soft outwardly, but in truth is utterly hard."

"Therefore boxing uses softness to overcome hardness, and thereby hits the center."

"How could boxing ever not use energy? If it did not use energy, how could the whole body move? Only, it is founded on the utmost great and utmost hard energy, and by straight cultivation does it no harm — that is all."

"One yin, one yang — one must surely turn them by the central fist (zhong quan). The central fist is neither leaning nor tilted; that is, the central energy of my heart (not stagnant, not ceasing, not awry, not departing, neither leaning nor tilted — this is the central energy), the so-called flood-like vital energy."

"This energy travels within the hands and feet; neither hard nor soft, it is naturally at ease."

"Vast and flowing, naturally one energy — light as willow catkins, firm as metal and stone; in tiger-fierceness it rivals ferocity, in eagle-soaring it rivals speed; in moving it is like the flow of water, in stopping it is equal to a mountain standing." "With an empty and nimble heart, cultivate the hard-within energy."

"A ball of great-harmony primal energy in the chest fills and encircles the four limbs, utterly soft and utterly hard, truly possessing the virtue of Qian's vigor and Kun's compliance. When it is still, yin and yang are stored there, with no trace to seek; when it moves, it seems utterly soft, yet in truth is utterly hard. Hardness and softness both present — this is called: yin and yang joining in virtue."

"In movement seeming soft yet truly hard, the spirit hidden within and not revealed — this is the highest grade."

"Kun is utterly soft, yet in moving it is hard." "Softness and compliance are aided by hardness and straightness."

"Qian is hard, Kun is soft; yin and yang are used together, neither leaning nor tilted, with no excess and no falling short."

· 297 · "Yin and yang used mutually — this is what the heavenly way stores; movement and stillness without bias — therein is your strength."

"When long practiced and utterly familiar, then rising and falling, advancing and retreating, and turning are free, and light and heavy, empty and full, hard and soft all issue together."

"Let men come to insult from all four sides: this body relies wholly on empty nimbleness, and the organs and frame have nothing they do not take heed of... let your cunning and trickery spring up as it may, hardness and softness arise of themselves."

"Boxing is named after tai chi. The ancients must have deeply understood the principle of tai chi, and then, throughout the whole body's above and below, left and right, front and back, with the hands and feet turning and moving, made manifest what tai chi contains; they established the name and fixed it as an established rule. Its meaning is most refined, its method most strict... Though it is said that boxing is a minor art, yet the great way of tai chi is present in it... Later men, in their affairs not taking the ancients as masters, either drift into wild arrogance or fall into leaning and bias; and to seek one who is neither hard nor soft, exactly fitting and just right, in accord with the principle of tai chi — this too is high and hard indeed."

"Yu's court held to the center; the Confucian school had its one thread running through; beyond this there is nothing more contained... To be divinely clear about it rests with the man."

"Yet since hardness and softness are divided, their issuing and use differ. When the four limbs are stirred and energy appears in the outward form, while within one holds still and heavy — this is the hard posture. When energy gathers within and outwardly appears light and harmonious — this is the soft posture. In using hardness one must not lack softness; without softness, the encirclement is not swift. In using softness one must not lack hardness; without hardness, the pressing advance is not quick. When hardness and softness aid one another, then sticking, wandering, connecting, following, soaring, flashing, shaking, emptying, rolling, throwing, squeezing, pressing — all attain their naturalness. Hardness and softness must not be used one-sidedly; in martial use, how can this be neglected!"

10. Slow first, then fast; fast and again slow "From beginning to end, one must move slowly and gently. As slow as one can be, be slow; when slowness reaches ten parts of practice, one can be nimble to ten parts. Only when nimbleness reaches the ten-parts mark can the enemy not keep up with me, and instead find my art strange and extraordinary — this is man's constant feeling; yet they little know it is the effect of the work of being slow first."

"In each technique, the five organs and hundred bones follow the natural momentum, and the energies of yin-yang and the five elements [...] · 298 · [...] move within it, as it is said: 'In movement yang is born, in stillness yin is born; one movement, one stillness, each is the root of the other.' And as it is said: 'Within yang there is yin, within yin there is yang.' This is precisely the original nature of tai chi chuan."

"There are three levels of practice in the steps of training tai chi chuan: the first step, when learning, one should be slow, but slow must not mean dullness; the second step, after practice one becomes fast, but fast must not mean confusion; the third step, after fast one again becomes slow — this is softness; when softness is long, hardness is naturally within it, and this is hardness and softness aiding one another." (This one item is a saying of Chen Fuyuan.)

11. Darting, running, leaping; suddenly up, suddenly down "Green Dragon Emerges from Water is the method of advancing straight and level-leaping; the left foot follows the right foot in leaping forward. In the crotch, the Huiyin and Changqiang forces rise along with the top-head energy; the forward leap is like a nimble cat pouncing on a rat — pure spirit, both empty and nimble."

"Guidance for beginners: after wringing down the fingertips, immediately follow with Green Dragon Emerges from Water. In the seam between the two postures, first loosen and sink the right shoulder, the right half of the body sinks along with it, and the lower foot again surges up to leap forward. Before the leap, the right hand grips like the tip of a whip, wishing to strike forward; first draw back, then from behind turn up and forward, circling one great circle to strike, and the body leaps forward along with it. The secret of the leap: the front hand leads forward, and the rear right foot's Yinbai, Dadun, Lidui, Qiaoyin, and Xiaxi all use force. The force passes from the sole of the foot through Yongquan to the heel, turns up, and reverses upward: Weizhong, Dianmen, Chengfu, Huantiao, slanting into Fubian, rising past Hunmen, Pohu, to Fufen, then slanting up again, from Quyuan through Xiaohai, slanting into Zhigou, Yangchi, turning over all along the way. Spread the hand open, bind the five fingers together, the right hand leads the body leaping forward, the left foot presses down with force, and following the right hand all reach forward; the left hand also follows the body forward. After the foot lands, the left hand settles to rest in front of the right breast.

Inner force: the whole right half of the body uses the right-turning force (right-turning is forward-turning, turning from inside outward). The right hand uses the silk-reeling force rising from the armpit, winding slantwise from inside outward to the fingertips; the right foot likewise uses the silk-reeling force, winding forward to the root of the thigh, rising to meet Fubian, all rising together to Fufen, dividing to the armpit, winding slantwise to the fingertips. The left hand and left foot must use the reverse-turning force, and only then can they follow along · 299 · The right hand and right foot turning in a circle and then leaping forward arise wholly from the heart. When the heart's force lifts once, above the top-head energy holds and guides, in the middle the cinnabar-field force issues, rising toward the right half of the body; below, the two feet — the right foot uses the leaping method, the right sole pressing hard and pushing back. Before the leap, all is stored force, gathering essence and concentrating spirit, binding together its energy. At the moment of leaping, it is purely a forward pouncing force, going straight on. The right hand carries the turn and carries the advance, like a sparrowhawk pouncing on a quail, a goshawk seizing a cunning rabbit — its will single, its spirit concentrated, its advance swift, its energy (energy is daring power) steady. The Jade Maiden Works the Shuttle's level-leaping body method: this too is a level-leaping method, and the farther the better. All must be done according to one's own strength; one must attain an easy, untroubled air, and not reveal any straining effort — that is best."

"Its inner force has its source farthest away: from Pucan it reverses upward, crossing the back and behind the shoulder to Fufen, and on to the right fingers."

"Jade Maiden Works the Shuttle is the forward silk-reeling level-leaping method... its advance is like the wind... the hand method, the step method, the turning method — the faster the better... Though above one relies on the hand, below one relies even more on the foot; when the foot is swift, the hand's swiftness is even more manifest... From the beginning posture to the end posture, though the right hand and right foot use the forward silk-reeling method, yet the method of the whole body is all reverse-turning force, advancing three times in succession, all as advancing steps. As for the inner force, from the top-head energy down to the five toes, the method is all the same as before; from first to last the right hand and right foot are the master, and the left hand and left foot assist them. When the right hand turns forward, the left hand must be turning in reverse — the silk-reeling force is that which one cannot for a moment depart from. The right hand takes turning a great circle as its form; when the practice is long, naturally small is better.

This posture is a great turning-the-body method; it follows on from Part the Wild Horse's Mane. The right hand, taking advantage of its being below, cannot pause for a moment, and so at once uses the silk-reeling force with the right hand to grip from below upward, flying slantwise like the wind toward the east all along the way, the fingers like steel awls; it also relies entirely on the right foot behind keeping up with the right hand, also using the forward silk-reeling force to hold to the rising posture, spreading the body method greatly, striving to advance three great steps eastward in succession, only then completing one great circle of about eight or nine feet. Especially one must raise the top-head energy well; the crotch force must not be full, and the body follows the right hand like a phoenix bird flying swiftly in advance, unable to be checked, the foot landing sticking to the ground and rising at once.

The completed posture of Jade Maiden Works the Shuttle seems much like Robing and Tucking the Garment, but in truth it is greatly different: that one does not turn the body, concentrating the mind on working the right hand and right foot, its energy tranquil, its spirit [...] · 300 · …calm; here, however, one turns the body and moves the hands and feet to protect oneself and repel the enemy, and since speed is the aim, the breath is fierce and the spirit hurried. Unless one ordinarily possesses real skill, and in the crisis drives breath through the whole body above and below, one cannot attain complete safety. Why? Because one goes out among a great crowd and with few opposes many, as though no one were beside him. Only one born with divine courage, whose gall is upright, whose breath is firm, and whose practice is thoroughly ripe, can therefore sweep all before him with ease."

"He turns, draws, turns and strikes, breaking out of the heavy encirclement, like the Weaving Girl working her loom. This body advances straight; who can match its swiftness? A single sliver of spirit moving—rare since ancient times."

"The two-rising kick (erqi tui) is a leaping method… What is meant by 'two risings'? The left and right feet in succession, together, leave the ground four or five feet and spring up; hence it is called 'kicking two risings.' …Yet one must first kick the left foot up with fierce force, and afterwards the right toes kick high, the instep level. The two-rising is purely a method of the whole body rising and lifting; the body method and the mind's strength lift upward, the whole body's spirit is roused, all leap up into the air, and only when the right foot can rise above the head-top is the form correct. The body follows the crown-strength and is urged upward; the higher the better; there are those who leap above the head-top—this cannot be done without a light body and great strength. …The upper body rises upward, and the lower body the more must use force to follow it up; the method of rising is that both feet must first stamp downward with force—the heavier the stamp, the higher the body rises."

"When the mind's strength once takes the lead, the five organs and hundred bones all rise with it."

"Both feet rise in linked succession; the whole body leaps into mid-air."

"The central breath is raised, the backbone strength is firm; the linked two-risings soar upward."

"What is meant by 'falling into the fork' (diecha): the body falls down from mid-air, the two legs split apart—this is 'falling into the fork.' In this figure the left leg extends open, the right leg is bent and held; this is the 'single falling fork.' As for the 'double falling fork,' without using the leaping method one cannot rise; it is not like the single falling fork, where one need only bring the left heel forward in a closing movement, open the right knee outward, and with force flip the right heel—then one rises and falls at once. It is somewhat easier than the other; hence used it too can overcome. And today all boxing masters do thus; for the present we follow it."

"The falling fork and the two-risings echo and answer each other: the two-risings go from below upward, flying into mid-air; this one comes from mid-air downward, the two legs touching the ground. A natural echoing, not forced to fit—such was the strictness of the ancient men's law of creating boxing."

"Strike high to alarm, take low—you must remember this; the left foot grazing the ground, the stamp benefits itself."

"It is not the shoulder and elbow that can defeat the enemy; a single foot kicks down the Phoenix Terrace."

"Were this body not made a man of iron, how would there come a sound of metal and stone when it is cast to the ground?"

"Breaking the encirclement lies in a single stamp; without great skill one cannot overcome a man with one foot."

"Stamping one heel (deng yi gen): I kick the enemy with my left foot; the enemy, with his right hand, strokes and holds my foot, wishing to twist it, to make me cry out in pain and fall to the ground, or lifting my foot, wishing to raise my whole body off the ground and then to bounce it up and strike it. I then follow the momentum, turning both hands over to press the ground, and with the right foot following the left leg, walk backward and upward, oversetting the enemy's right hand that presses my left foot—the difficulty is at once resolved. Or again, if the enemy presses my left foot, I then with my right foot stamp the enemy's right elbow-tip, or stamp his wrist-joint—both can resolve it. This is the general outline of 'stamping one heel.'

If a man comes to stamp me, I then take my left foot and step back one pace, to guard against his stamping my dove-tail (jiuwei) and below the chin-receptacle (chengjiang) down to the throat.

Yet to be cautious at the moment of the stamp is already late; better to be cautious at the moment when the previous posture is about to kick—if you see it can kick, then kick; if it cannot kick, then do not kick; do not rashly use its kick.

Even if there be a crack to seize, in kicking speed is prized, not slowness; it is prized to kick the tightly-closed acupoints, not to kick the broad thigh and thick flesh where it does not touch the painful, itching spot. This is the essential secret; the kicker must know it."

"The posture 'Wild Horse Parts its Mane': both hands grasp the ground and turn like flying, a single thread running through the middle with no leaning. Both hands brush upward along the ground, and the whole body above and below can guard itself; the central breath rises from the hundred-meetings point (baihui) above and runs down through the long-strength point (changqiang), as though threaded on one line. The two hands are like two rings, one above the other, dancing in alternation; its firmness cannot be broken, its sharpness has no equal, its turning has no interval—hence it can repel the enemy."

"The posture 'Spread-Brocade on the Ground' (pu di jin) echoes and answers the falling fork: the falling fork hangs in the air and drops straight down, the right foot stamping the ground with a sound of metal and stone, to stamp the enemy's foot; the left foot stamps the enemy's shin-bone, which can break his courage. The right hand spreads open the arm and brushes up along the ground, the left hand thrusts forward to push the enemy's chest; here, then, one sits back with the buttock and thigh to sit upon the man's knee, the right hand's fist bends with intent to strike forward, and the left leg spreads open—if one cannot win thus, both hands · 301 · …such was the strictness of the law of boxing."

"Strike high to alarm, take low—you must remember this; the left foot grazing the ground, the stamp benefits itself."

"It is not the shoulder and elbow that can defeat the enemy; a single foot kicks down the Phoenix Terrace."

"Were this body not made a man of iron, how would there come a sound of metal and stone when it is cast to the ground?"

"Breaking the encirclement lies in a single stamp; without great skill one cannot overcome a man with one foot."

"Stamping one heel (deng yi gen): I kick the enemy with my left foot; the enemy, with his right hand, strokes and holds my foot, wishing to twist it, to make me cry out in pain and fall to the ground, or lifting my foot, wishing to raise my whole body off the ground and then to bounce it up and strike it. I then follow the momentum, turning both hands over to press the ground, and with the right foot following the left leg, walk backward and upward, oversetting the enemy's right hand that presses my left foot—the difficulty is at once resolved. Or again, if the enemy presses my left foot, I then with my right foot stamp the enemy's right elbow-tip, or stamp his wrist-joint—both can resolve it. This is the general outline of 'stamping one heel.'

If a man comes to stamp me, I then take my left foot and step back one pace, to guard against his stamping my dove-tail (jiuwei) and below the chin-receptacle (chengjiang) down to the throat.

Yet to be cautious at the moment of the stamp is already late; better to be cautious at the moment when the previous posture is about to kick—if you see it can kick, then kick; if it cannot kick, then do not kick; do not rashly use its kick.

Even if there be a crack to seize, in kicking speed is prized, not slowness; it is prized to kick the tightly-closed acupoints, not to kick the broad thigh and thick flesh where it does not touch the painful, itching spot. This is the essential secret; the kicker must know it."

"The posture 'Wild Horse Parts its Mane': both hands grasp the ground and turn like flying, a single thread running through the middle with no leaning. Both hands brush upward along the ground, and the whole body above and below can guard itself; the central breath rises from the hundred-meetings point (baihui) above and runs down through the long-strength point (changqiang), as though threaded on one line. The two hands are like two rings, one above the other, dancing in alternation; its firmness cannot be broken, its sharpness has no equal, its turning has no interval—hence it can repel the enemy."

"The posture 'Spread-Brocade on the Ground' (pu di jin) echoes and answers the falling fork: the falling fork hangs in the air and drops straight down, the right foot stamping the ground with a sound of metal and stone, to stamp the enemy's foot; the left foot stamps the enemy's shin-bone, which can break his courage. The right hand spreads open the arm and brushes up along the ground, the left hand thrusts forward to push the enemy's chest; here, then, one sits back with the buttock and thigh to sit upon the man's knee, the right hand's fist bends with intent to strike forward, and the left leg spreads open—if one cannot win thus, both hands · 302 · …the right brushes toward the ground, using the sweeping-ground whip to sweep the lower shins of the crowd of enemies; then the difficulty resolves itself. Thus it echoes with things of its own kind. Again it echoes with 'Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg': the Golden Rooster raises the left leg upright, while here the left leg lies crosswise; the Golden Rooster knees a man with the right knee, and here too the right knee is bent and held; the Golden Rooster lets the left hand hang down and stretches the right arm upward, while here the right hand is bent and held and the left hand is stretched upward—hence they echo each other above and below. Again it echoes with the two-risings: the two-risings lift the body flying into mid-air, while here the body drops to the ground—hence again they make an echo above and below."

"Front and back, left and right, above and below, on all four sides—the turning and joining are nimble; slow and urgent keep pace together; strike high and take low, and each wish is gratified. …Rising to strike and dropping to strike must never be one-sided; feint to the east and strike to the west—left and right are both suitable. …Horizontal and vertical, toppled and leaning, sitting and standing tilted and upright, bowing forward and leaning back—the strange and the orthodox beget each other; whirling and leaning to the side, gathering and leaping all hit the mark (all have the central breath's release and gathering, governed within them)."

"The foot follows the hand's movement, revolving like a spirit—now up (hands and feet upward), now down (hands and feet downward); sometimes with-turning (shun) (using the with-twining method, its strength follows), sometimes against (ni) (using the reverse-turning method, its strength opposes)."

"'Tipping the Red Robe' (dao juan hong) is a retreating movement to evade left and right; 'White Goose Spreads its Wings' is a right-draw left-strike, and at the same time an upper-draw lower-strike method; 'Brush the Knee and Twist the Step' is six-sealings (above and below, front and back, left and right—all doors sealed) and four-avoidings (the four avoidings are east, west, south and north, leaving a man no crack to attack); 'Flash Through the Back' is a forward-flash (from behind flashing forward), backward-slip (when the rear cannot be pressed down, pressing hard makes one slip and fall) advancing-strike method; 'Grasp the Robe' and 'Single Whip' are both draw-one advance-one methods (this word 'advance' means advancing to strike); 'Moving Hands' is a left-right draw-one advance-one striking method; 'High Pat the Horse' is a left-arm back-bending elbow method; 'Left and Right Plant the Foot' is a lower-body forward-attacking stamping method; 'Middle Single Whip' is a left-right up-down hands-and-feet striking-together method; 'Strike the Ground Blow' is an attacking-low method, and behind the body at the same time a slipping-falling method. The secret is that the life-gate (mingmen), between the two kidneys in the middle of the two loins, is the hinge and pivot of the upper and lower body. Above and below the hinge all is reverse-turning strength; the body carries a sideways lean and holds; the right rear flank goes up, the left rear flank goes down; when the downward strength is good and the foot is planted firm, if a man is struck on the back, the body at once twists and turns—the swifter the better. If one can follow the foot method, then the man slips and falls of himself. The two-rising kick, the single kick, and the stamping of one heel are reverse-turning great body-turn methods, and with both feet · 303 · …attack methods (the hand serves as the foot, and the foot serves as the hand); 'Rolling-Hand Hammer' and 'Small Capture and Strike' are forward-attacking upper-and-lower methods; 'Embrace the Head and Push the Mountain' is a reverse-turning (referring to the body) advancing-pushing method; 'Single Whip' is a with-turning (with-turning also refers to the body method) left-and-right draw-strike method.

The above several tens of postures are for one man fighting a great battle against several tens of men; as for the method of evading the enemy, it does not go beyond above and below and the two sides—whichever side is tight, first loosen the encirclement on that side; when they come all together, as soon as the central breath moves, all are at once made to scatter. Without skill this cannot be done."

(Note: All the boxing postures mentioned above are postures of the Chen-style old frame; recorded here for reference.)

12. Firmness and Softness Both Extinguished, a Single Piece of Spirit Moving "When the skill of movement matures, then one transforms firmness into softness, and refines softness into firmness; when firmness and softness attain the mean, then yin and yang appear. Hence this boxing cannot be named by firmness, nor named by softness; it is simply named by the nameless name of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji)."

"When it is still, what yin and yang store leaves no trace to be seen; when it moves, it seems supremely soft, yet in truth is supremely firm; it seems supremely firm, yet in truth is supremely soft. Firmness and softness alternate in operation, with no end to be found."

"The principle of Taiji circulates, handed down who knows how many years; within it there is essential meaning—movement and stillness both without bias… Opening and closing are originally without fixity (lively and flowing), bending and stretching are linked in posture (yet have a definite order). Taiji divides into yin and yang; the spirit-dragon transforms without limit; heaven and earth are father and mother; they rub and wash softness and firmness; production and production truly never cease; the strange and the orthodox are no common thing. Qian and Kun are like the bellows-pipe; Taiji is one great bellows-bag; the causes of fullness and emptiness, waxing and waning, are all stored within it. To the very end it again begins from the start; one breath moves tension and slack; the formed returns to tracelessness; things and self are both forgotten."

"Closing and opening, firmness and softness follow nature; one raising and one lowering, the principle circles."
